name: aria2
popularity: ~25k+ GitHub stars, very widely deployed as an embedded engine (used by Motrix, many NAS vendors, etc.); maintenance is slow/low-activity upstream but the project is considered feature-complete and stable, so ecosystem tooling (AriaNg, aria2p, Motrix) continues to thrive around it years after last major release.
architecture: aria2c is a single long-running daemon process that does the actual downloading (HTTP/HTTPS/FTP/SFTP/BitTorrent/Metalink, segmented/multi-connection) and exposes control entirely through an RPC server, never a GUI. The RPC server (HttpListenCommand) speaks both JSON-RPC 2.0 and XML-RPC over the same HTTP port, plus JSON-RPC over WebSocket for push-style usage; protocol is auto-detected per request. Every download is identified by an opaque GID; state transitions and progress are queried by GID via tellStatus/tellActive/tellWaiting/tellStopped rather than pushed automatically unless the client uses the WebSocket transport, which lets aria2 emit onDownloadStart/onDownloadPause/onDownloadStop/onDownloadComplete/onDownloadError/onBtDownloadComplete notifications. Authentication is a single shared secret token (--rpc-secret) passed as the first RPC parameter (`token:SECRET`), no per-user accounts. Any number of independent frontends (CLI flags, AriaNg, Motrix, aria2p, custom scripts) can drive the same daemon concurrently because all state lives server-side in the daemon, not in any client.
standout_features: Full RPC surface with system.multicall for batching many calls in one round trip, and system.listMethods/listNotifications for client-side introspection/capability discovery
Per-download binary control files (<file>.aria2) that store piece bitfields and checksums next to the partial download, enabling resume even after an ungraceful kill, independent of any session file

--save-session writes all still-incomplete/errored downloads' URIs + per-download options to a plain text file on exit (or every --save-session-interval seconds); --input-file re-reads that same file format to resume a whole queue, effectively giving a human-readable/git-diffable queue snapshot

Every option (getOption/changeOption per-GID, getGlobalOption/changeGlobalOption globally) is settable at runtime through RPC, not just at process start, so a UI can let users tweak speed limits, segment counts, etc. live

Deliberately decouples 'engine that downloads' from 'thing that renders UI' — the daemon has zero UI code, which is exactly why dozens of unrelated frontends could be built against it without any coordination with the aria2 maintainers
pitfalls_to_avoid: XML-RPC support exists but is legacy/deprecated in practice — don't build new integrations against it, JSON-RPC (HTTP or WS) is the one that matters

Session files (--save-session) are a periodic/on-exit snapshot, not a transactional log — a hard crash between saves loses queue state even though per-file .aria2 control files still allow resuming the bytes; don't treat the session file alone as durable state
The shared single secret token model has no concept of per-user permissions or audit trail — fine for a single-user daemon, not a template for multi-tenant auth
ideas_for_kurio: Formalize Kurio.Server's SignalR hub methods as a small, versioned, documented RPC surface (AddDownload, Pause, Resume, Remove, ChangePriority/Position, GetStatus, GetGlobalStats, ChangeOptions) so that any future frontend (CLI, TUI, third-party) can drive Kurio without needing SignalR-specific knowledge — mirror aria2's tellActive/tellWaiting/tellStopped split as three queue-status endpoints
Add a GetCapabilities/ListMethods-equivalent REST endpoint so new UIs can introspect what the running server version supports, easing future plugin/extension work

Adopt aria2's per-item resume model: persist per-download resume metadata (segment offsets, checksums-in-progress) in its own small file/row keyed by download ID, separate from the overall queue snapshot, so a crash mid-download doesn't require re-downloading segments already verified — check whether Kurio.Core's current JSON state persistence already does this per-download or only as one big blob

Add a --save-session-interval equivalent: periodic (e.g. every N seconds) durable flush of the in-flight queue state in addition to on-shutdown save, so an unclean process exit (crash, OOM-kill, container restart) loses at most N seconds of queue changes

Expose runtime-changeable global and per-download options (speed limit, max connections/segments, retry policy) via the REST/SignalR API the same way aria2 exposes changeOption/changeGlobalOption, instead of requiring a restart to apply new settings

Support a human-readable export/import of the download queue (URIs + per-item options), similar to aria2's --input-file text format, to satisfy the 'import/export' backlog item and let users batch-add or migrate queues via a text file

Push events over SignalR for lifecycle transitions (download started/paused/completed/failed) using named events analogous to onDownloadStart/onDownloadComplete/onDownloadError, rather than only progress-percentage updates, so a thin frontend can react to state changes without polling

name: Motrix
popularity: ~48k+ GitHub stars historically one of the most popular cross-platform download-manager GUIs; recent activity has slowed (project largely feature-frozen), but still widely used as the reference example of 'GUI wrapping aria2'.
architecture: Motrix is an Electron app: the main process supervises a bundled aria2c binary as a child process (EngineSupervisor), and the renderer (Vue UI) talks to aria2 exclusively through JSON-RPC over WebSocket via an Aria2RpcClient — never by touching the child process directly. Startup is staged: verify the bundled aria2 binary's version/feature set, generate an aria2.conf via an Aria2ConfigBuilder (picking a free RPC port, secret, download dirs, etc.), spawn the process with the built config/args, then open the RPC WebSocket connection. A background health check runs periodically (~every 30s) to detect a dead/hung engine and can restart it or produce a diagnostics report (checks: bundled binary present, feature support, port availability, process ownership — i.e. confirming a process squatting on the port is actually Motrix's own before killing it). Notably, Motrix v2 does not fully rely on aria2's own session/control files for its task list UI — it layers a SQLite database on top to store task metadata/history, using aria2 purely as the transfer engine underneath.
standout_features: Clean separation of 'engine lifecycle management' (spawn/health-check/restart/config-generation) from 'engine control' (RPC client) as distinct components/classes

Self-diagnostics flow (Diagnostics dialog: bundled aria2 check, feature check, port check, process-ownership check, RPC communication check) exposed directly to end users when something goes wrong, rather than a silent failure
Verifies process ownership before offering to force-kill a process on its RPC port — avoids accidentally killing an unrelated process that happens to occupy the same port
Own persistence layer (SQLite) for richer task metadata/history than the underlying engine natively tracks, decoupling UI-facing state from engine-native session state
pitfalls_to_avoid: Coupling UI database state with engine state risks drift/desync if the two aren't kept reconciled on every startup (e.g. engine reports a GID Motrix's DB doesn't know about, or vice versa after a crash) — needs an explicit reconciliation step on launch

Bundling a specific engine binary version ties the app to that engine's exact RPC/feature set and requires the app to re-verify compatibility (version/feature checks) on every startup, adding real startup latency and failure surface
A generic 30s poll-based health check can be slow to notice a hung (not crashed) process; would benefit from a lighter heartbeat RPC call rather than only process-alive checks
ideas_for_kurio: Since Kurio.Core is an in-process library rather than an external daemon, Kurio doesn't need Motrix's spawn/supervise-external-process complexity — but it should still borrow the 'reconcile persisted state against actual engine state on startup' step: on Kurio.Server startup, reconcile the JSON-persisted download records against Kurio.Core's actual in-memory/resumable segment state before exposing them to the dashboard

Add a self-diagnostics endpoint/page in Kurio.Web mirroring Motrix's Diagnostics dialog: checks like 'disk space for download dir', 'write permission', 'network reachability', 'stale partial files without matching queue entries' — surfaced to the user instead of failing silently

If Kurio ever adds a lightweight local health/heartbeat signal for long-running downloads (e.g. a per-download watchdog that flags a segment worker as stuck if no byte progress in N seconds), that's a more responsive analogue to Motrix's health check than pure process-alive polling

Consider Motrix's pattern of storing richer queue/task metadata (history, tags, notes) in a small SQLite/EF Core store on the server side, separate from the low-level per-segment resume data in Kurio.Core, so Kurio.Web can show download history/analytics without bloating the engine's resume-state format

name: AriaNg
popularity: ~11k+ GitHub stars, actively used as 'the' generic web UI for any aria2 instance; moderate ongoing maintenance (mayswind), long-lived and stable rather than fast-moving.
architecture: AriaNg has zero backend of its own — it is pure static HTML/CSS/JS shipped in three build flavors (standard, for hosting on any web server with on-demand asset loading; all-in-one, a single self-contained HTML file; and AriaNg Native, an Electron-style wrapper for local/offline use without a browser). All application state (which aria2 RPC endpoint(s) to talk to, host/port/secret, UI preferences) is configured client-side and stored in the browser (localStorage), then the page talks directly to one or more aria2 daemons' JSON-RPC endpoints over HTTP or WebSocket from the browser's JS. It supports connecting to and switching between multiple aria2 RPC hosts from the same static deployment, and minimizes bandwidth by requesting only incremental/delta status updates rather than re-fetching full state each poll.
standout_features: Entirely serverless frontend — deployable by dropping files on any static file host (or opening the single HTML file locally), proving that a sufficiently well-designed RPC API needs no bespoke backend glue code per-frontend
Multi-endpoint support: one AriaNg deployment can be pointed at several different aria2 daemons and switch between them, since connection config is just client-side state, not baked into a build
Deliberately requests incremental data rather than full snapshots on each poll cycle to keep the UI responsive over slow/metered connections
Full coverage of aria2's global + per-download options through generic forms driven off the RPC's own option schema, rather than hand-coding a form per option
pitfalls_to_avoid: Storing the RPC secret token in browser localStorage/URL is inherently exposed to anything with page access (XSS, browser extensions, shared machines) — acceptable for a trusted single-user LAN daemon, not a pattern to copy for a multi-user server exposed to the internet
No server-side authorization/session model at all — every permission decision is 'does the browser have the secret', which doesn't map to a real multi-user product like Kurio might become

A fully static, no-backend frontend can't do anything the RPC API doesn't already expose (e.g. no server-side aggregation/caching) — every feature has to be pushed down into the RPC surface design up front
ideas_for_kurio: Design Kurio.Server's REST/SignalR API to be rich and generic enough (full CRUD + option schema + queue reordering + stats) that a future minimal/alternate frontend (e.g. a lightweight static page, a mobile app, a CLI) could be built against it without any new server code — treat Kurio.Web (Blazor) as just one client of that API, not the only possible one

Add a generic 'describe available download/global options' endpoint (name, type, default, constraints) so Kurio.Web (and any future client) can render option-editing forms dynamically instead of hand-coding a form per setting whenever a new option is added to Kurio.Core

If/when Kurio needs to support connecting one dashboard instance to multiple Kurio.Server backends (e.g. home server + NAS), take AriaNg's approach of storing the list of known server endpoints client-side and letting the user switch between them, rather than hard-coding a single server URL

For efficiency, make SignalR progress broadcasts delta-only (changed fields since last tick) rather than full download-state snapshots each tick, especially once many concurrent downloads are running, mirroring AriaNg's 'incremental data' bandwidth optimization

Do not copy AriaNg's client-stored-secret auth model as-is for Kurio if multi-user/remote-exposure is ever a goal — plan for proper ASP.NET Core auth (cookies/JWT) on the API even though today's dashboard is trusted/local, so the API design doesn't calcify around a single shared secret

name: Gopeed
popularity: ~26,000 GitHub stars, ~1,700 forks, actively maintained (commits as recent as within the last day; releases across Windows/macOS/Linux/Android/iOS/Docker)
language: Go (core/backend) + Flutter/Dart (UI, all platforms including web) + JavaScript/Goja (extensions)
architecture: Single Go binary hosts everything: a download engine (pkg/download), a REST API server (pkg/rest, using gorilla/mux), and an embedded JS extension VM (Goja). The Flutter app is a thin client that talks to the Go backend purely over HTTP/REST — there is no WebSocket/SignalR-style push channel; the desktop client instead uses a local IPC channel (Unix domain socket on macOS/Linux, TCP on Windows) to the same REST server, and the web deployment (Docker) serves the Flutter web build directly from the Go binary alongside the API (embedded FS with cache headers, plus /fs/tasks and /fs/extensions virtual filesystems for serving downloaded/extension files). Protocols are abstracted behind a `Fetcher`/`FetcherManager` interface pair: `FetcherManager` registers URL/file/base64 `SchemeFilter`s per protocol (http, bt, ...) and builds/stores/restores `Fetcher` instances; each `Fetcher` implements Setup/Resolve/Start/Patch/Pause/Close/Stats/Meta/Progress/Wait, decoupling task orchestration from protocol specifics. Persistence is pluggable via a `Storage` interface with two implementations: `MemStorage` (in-memory map, for testing/embedded use) and `BoltStorage` (bbolt embedded KV store, file `gopeed.db`, JSON-marshaled values per bucket/key) — tasks, extensions, extension-storage, and config all live in separate 'buckets' inside one Bolt file, and on startup the downloader lists the tasks bucket and calls each FetcherManager's `Restore()` to rehydrate in-flight/paused downloads. Auth is optional (API token header `X-Api-Token`, or Basic-auth-derived AES-GCM encrypted bearer token for the web UI with 7-day expiry).
standout_features: Clean Fetcher/FetcherManager interface: protocols self-register SchemeFilters (by URL scheme, file extension, or base64 mime type) so the core doesn't need protocol-specific branching to pick a handler for a given link
Pluggable Storage interface (Mem vs Bolt) with bucket/key JSON persistence — trivial to swap backends, and restore-on-boot is just `Storage.List(bucket)` + FetcherManager.Restore() per task

JavaScript extension system (Goja ECMAScript 5.1 VM) with declarative manifest.json: scripts declare an `event` (onResolve/onStart/onError/onDone), a `match` block (Chrome-extension-style URL match patterns + request label matching), and an `entry` JS file; a fresh JS engine+context is spun up per trigger and the extension registers handlers via `gopeed.events.onResolve(fn)` etc.

Extensions are distributed as plain git repositories (installed via `InstallExtensionByGit`, using go-git PlainClone with depth=1, supporting a `repo_url#subdirectory` syntax and proxy config) — no central marketplace/registry service required, and extensions declare their own repository URL in manifest.json for one-click update checks

Per-extension persistent KV storage (`ContextStorage` in JS) and per-extension typed settings (string/number/boolean with options list, merged intelligently across upgrades so old values survive version bumps while new/removed settings are reconciled)
Extension dev mode: install-by-folder with `devMode` flag skips copying into the extensions dir and instead runs directly from the source path, enabling live-reload style extension development
onError hook gets a special `Continue()` capability (auto-retry/resume) not exposed to other hooks — a deliberate least-privilege API surface per event type

Outbound webhooks (DOWNLOAD_DONE/DOWNLOAD_ERROR) as a separate, simpler notification channel from the extension system — POSTs a JSON payload with the full cloned Task to configured URLs, decoupled from the polling REST API

REST API surface is small and resource-oriented: /api/v1/resolve (protocol-agnostic link resolution before task creation), /api/v1/tasks (+ batch, pause/continue singular and bulk, patch), /api/v1/tasks/{id}/stats, /api/v1/extensions CRUD + settings + switch (enable/disable) + update-check/update, /api/v1/webhook/test, and a generic /api/v1/proxy passthrough endpoint
ideas_for_kurio: Add a formal `IFetcher`/`IFetcherManager`-style abstraction in Kurio.Core if not already present: SchemeFilter-like matching (by URL scheme / extension / mime) so adding FTP or magnet/BT later doesn't require touching the HTTP-specific engine code

Add an /api/resolve endpoint that resolves a URL to file name/size/resumability before a task is created, separate from actual task creation — useful for UI preview and for a future extension/plugin hook point

Design a JS (or C# Roslyn scripting / NuGet plugin) extension system around explicit lifecycle hooks mirroring onResolve/onStart/onError/onDone, with a declarative manifest (JSON) describing URL match patterns and entry point, distributed as git repos rather than a bespoke package registry — directly addresses the 'plugin/extension system' backlog item

Give extensions/plugins their own isolated KV storage namespace and a typed settings schema (string/number/bool with validation) surfaced generically in the Blazor dashboard as an auto-generated settings form

Add outbound webhook support (task done/error POST to user-configured URLs) as a lightweight integration point distinct from SignalR — useful for headless/server deployments where nobody has a live dashboard connection open

Adopt a Storage interface abstraction (in-memory vs persistent) in Kurio.Core so JSON-file persistence can be swapped for an embedded KV store (e.g. LiteDB or a bucketed JSON store) without touching engine logic; keep the current JSON persistence but formalize it behind this interface for testability

Support installing/updating 'site handler' extensions via git URL with an optional #subdirectory suffix and a depth=1 shallow clone, enabling community-contributed link resolvers (e.g., for cloud-storage share links) without app redeploys
Consider an API-token header auth mode (simple shared-secret via header) as a lightweight alternative to full auth for headless/automation use of the REST API

Note the resume/restore pattern: on startup, list all persisted tasks and call a protocol-specific Restore() to rebuild in-memory Fetcher/download state — verify Kurio.Core's own resume path follows the same 'restore metadata then re-attach fetcher' shape rather than re-deriving everything from scratch

name: Brisk
popularity: ~1.5k GitHub stars, 59 forks, 1,151+ commits on main, 38 open issues, 1 open PR — actively maintained, Flutter SDK v3.32.0
architecture: Brisk is a Flutter desktop app (Windows/macOS/Linux, distributed via Flatpak/Snap/AUR/direct) with a fully custom download engine written in Dart on top of the stock `http` package — no aria2 or other external download utility is shelled out to. There is no separate server process: the download engine runs in-process (Dart isolates are the natural mechanism for parallel segment fetches, keeping the UI thread free), and persistent session/resume state is written to disk so paused/interrupted downloads can be resumed. A companion `brisk-browser-extension` repo (Chrome/Edge/Opera/Firefox, on official add-on stores) captures browser download requests and M3U8 stream URLs and forwards them into the running Brisk app; exact IPC transport (likely a local loopback listener in the app) wasn't documented in the README and would require reading the extension's source to confirm, but the pattern mirrors IDM/JDownloader-style 'browser posts captured link to local desktop app' integrations. Queueing/scheduling is a first-class feature: downloads can be grouped into queues and scheduled to start at specific times (e.g., overnight/off-peak).
standout_features: Dynamic connection spawn: downloads start with a single connection and additional connections are added on the fly only as needed, rather than always opening N connections up front

Dynamic connection reuse: once a connection finishes its assigned byte range, it is immediately reassigned to help another still-active connection's remaining range instead of sitting idle, keeping the active-connection count and aggregate speed pegged near the target until the whole file completes
Automatic detection and reset of hanging/stalled connections
Browser extension integration that captures normal download requests AND M3U8 adaptive-stream manifests directly from the page, letting Brisk download and reassemble streaming video
Soft-subtitle handling/integration when downloading video content captured from streaming sites
Bulk link capture: extension can extract every download link from a selected block of page text and hand them to Brisk as a batch
Download queues with time-based scheduling (start queues at a specific time to hit off-peak bandwidth windows)
Polished, lightweight UI with multiple themes (catppuccin, tokyo night) and system tray integration across platforms
Custom global hotkey to capture a URL straight from the clipboard without touching the browser extension
ideas_for_kurio: Add dynamic connection reuse to Kurio.Core's segmented downloader: when a connection finishes its assigned byte range early (fast source), reassign it to steal/split the remaining range of the slowest still-running connection instead of leaving it idle — this is the single most-praised Brisk engine behavior and directly improves aggregate throughput on uneven links

Start new downloads with 1 connection and ramp connection count up dynamically based on observed throughput/segment completion rate, rather than always opening the configured max connections immediately — reduces server-side rate-limit/ban risk and matches user expectations from Brisk/IDM

Add a 'stalled connection watchdog' in Kurio.Core: detect segments with no byte progress for N seconds and automatically cancel+re-issue that segment's request (already close to what Polly retry gives you, but should trigger on stall detection, not just HTTP failure)

Build a lightweight companion browser extension (WebExtension, Chrome/Firefox/Edge) that POSTs captured download URLs (and detected M3U8 manifests) to a local Kurio.Server REST endpoint — this is a much lower-effort integration than full browser plugin architectures and is exactly the pattern Brisk uses to get 'click a link, it appears in the download manager' UX

Add bulk-add-from-text: a dashboard action (and matching REST endpoint) that accepts a pasted blob of text/HTML and extracts every URL, letting users queue many links at once — trivial to implement and highly requested UX pattern

Add download queues with scheduled start times (e.g., 'start this queue at 02:00') as a first backlog item for the scheduling feature already listed as open backlog — model it as a Queue entity with a NextRunAt and a background hosted service that flips queued items to Active

Consider M3U8/HLS capture+reassembly as a scoped follow-up to the existing yt-dlp backlog item: even without yt-dlp, an M3U8 downloader (fetch manifest, download segments in parallel via the same engine, concatenate) covers a common 'download this streaming video' use case with pure HTTP, before investing in full yt-dlp shelling

For the SignalR dashboard, borrow Brisk's UX detail of surfacing 'active connections' and per-connection state (idle/reassigned/downloading) in the progress view, not just aggregate percent/speed — makes the connection-reuse behavior visible and builds user trust in the engine
pitfalls_to_avoid: Brisk's browser-extension-to-app IPC transport wasn't documented publicly in the README/search results I could access; don't assume a specific protocol (native messaging vs. localhost HTTP) without reading the extension source directly if exact parity is desired

Dynamic connection reuse adds real complexity (need to track remaining ranges per segment and safely hand off an in-flight connection to a different byte range) — prototype it as an isolated strategy behind a feature flag in Kurio.Core rather than baking it into the core segment-scheduling loop right away

Scheduling/queues need persistence and a resilient background trigger (survive app/server restarts) — don't implement as an in-memory timer only, since Kurio.Server should survive restarts per its stated design goals

name: AB Download Manager (ab-download-manager)
language: Kotlin (Compose Multiplatform for UI; core engine is pure Kotlin/coroutines, no UI deps)
popularity: 17.5k stars, 904 forks, actively maintained (commits/releases within the last week as of Aug 2026), Apache-2.0 license. Companion repos: browser-integration (229 stars, TS/WebExtension), website. This is very likely the project the user meant by 'very popular recently' given its growth curve.
architecture: Multi-module Gradle project cleanly separating the download engine from UI: `downloader/core` (pure Kotlin engine: connection handling, part/segment management, persistence, queueing, speed limiting), `downloader/monitor` (read-only state/observability layer exposing `IDownloadMonitor`/`IDownloadItemState` flows for UI or remote consumers without coupling to engine internals), `desktop` and `android/app` (Compose Multiplatform UI consuming the shared `shared` module), and `integration/server` (an embedded HTTP server, default port 15151, documented by a root `REST-API.yml` OpenAPI spec with endpoints `POST /add` (add a link, optionally with headers/downloadPage), `GET /queues` (list queues), `POST /start-headless-download` (add a task programmatically with folder/name/queueId) — this is the local RPC surface the browser extension and external tools talk to). Everything in the engine is built on Kotlin coroutines/Flow: `DownloadManager`/`Downloader`/`DownloadJob` orchestrate `PartDownloader`/`HttpPartDownloader` (segment-level workers) and `HLSPartDownloader` (first-class HLS/m3u8 streaming media downloader alongside HTTP, sharing the same job/queue/monitor abstractions via `HLSDownloadItem`/`HLSDownloader`). Persistence is flat-file JSON: `DownloadListFileStorage` writes one `{id}.json` per download item (metadata) and `PartListFileStorage` writes a parallel `{id}.json` per download recording its `Parts`/segment ranges (offsets, downloaded bytes per part) so paused/interrupted downloads can resume by reconstructing byte-range requests. All writes go through `TransactionalFileSaver`, which writes to a `.tmp` file then does an atomic rename (`tryAtomicMove`) to avoid corrupting state on crash/power loss — no SQLite/DB engine, just crash-safe JSON files. Disk space is pre-reserved via an `expect/actual` `SparseFile` abstraction (platform-specific sparse-file allocation on desktop vs Android) rather than zero-filling. Queueing (`QueueManager`/`DownloadQueue`/`ManualDownloadQueue`) supports multiple independent queues (a reserved default 'Main' queue plus user-created ones with IDs above a reserved threshold) with scheduling (`ScheduleTimes`) and emits `QueueEvent`s via a `SharedFlow`. Speed limiting is implemented via a custom Okio `Throttler` (`OkioCustomizedThrottler`/`SpeedLimiter`) wrapping the byte stream rather than sleep-based limiting. Proxy support is a pluggable `ProxyStrategyProvider`/`AutoConfigurableProxyProvider` abstraction supporting system-proxy detection.
standout_features: Embedded local REST API (port 15151, OpenAPI-documented) purely for browser-extension/automation hand-off, decoupled from the main UI's own IPC — add-link, list-queues, and headless-add-with-folder/name/queue endpoints

Browser extension (Firefox + Chrome) adds a context-menu 'Download With AB DM' entry, auto-captures download-intent links, and shows a 'Download Selected' popup for multi-link batch capture from a page selection

Clean 3-tier engine/monitor/UI split: `downloader/core` has zero UI dependencies; `downloader/monitor` is a separate module exposing read-only reactive state (Flow-based) for any consumer (desktop UI, Android UI, or theoretically a server), which is architecturally very close to what a SignalR hub needs to broadcast
First-class HLS/m3u8 streaming-media download support built on the same DownloadItem/Job/Queue/Monitor abstractions as plain HTTP — not a bolt-on

Crash-safe persistence via write-tmp-then-atomic-rename for every state file, with per-download JSON metadata file + separate per-download JSON parts/segments file (clean separation of 'what' vs 'how far along')
Sparse-file pre-allocation abstracted behind a multiplatform `expect/actual` interface so desktop and Android get platform-appropriate space reservation
Multiple independent, schedulable download queues with reserved ID ranges to leave room for future built-in queues without ID collisions

Rich typed exception hierarchy for resumability edge cases (e.g. `ServerResumeSupportChangeException`, `ServerPartIsNotTheSameAsWeExpectException`, `FileChangedException`) that explicitly models cases where a paused download must fall back to restarting because the remote resource changed
pitfalls_to_avoid: Do not couple the monitor/broadcast layer to engine internals — ab-download-manager's separate `downloader/monitor` module (with its own `IDownloadItemState` types) exists specifically so UI/remote layers never depend on live engine job objects; Kurio.Server's SignalR hub should broadcast a similarly decoupled DTO/state-snapshot type, not raw engine entities
Naive JSON persistence without atomic writes risks corrupting state files on crash mid-write; always write-to-temp-then-rename

Treating HLS/streaming downloads as an afterthought bolted onto the HTTP path leads to duplicated queue/resume/monitor logic later — if Kurio ever adds yt-dlp/streaming support, design the job abstraction to accommodate a non-range-based downloader type from the start

A local RPC surface for browser integration needs explicit versioning/auth even on localhost (extension and app versions can drift) — the OpenAPI spec here is unauthenticated on localhost, which is a reasonable but explicit tradeoff worth calling out rather than accidentally inheriting
ideas_for_kurio: Add a documented, versioned local/embedded REST endpoint set explicitly for browser-extension hand-off (e.g. POST /api/browser/add-link with link/headers/referrer/suggestedName, GET /api/queues) separate from the main dashboard API, mirroring the add/queues/start-headless-download trio, and publish an OpenAPI spec file at the repo root the way ab-download-manager does with REST-API.yml

Build a minimal Chrome/Firefox WebExtension (Manifest V3) that adds a context-menu 'Download with Kurio' item and posts captured links to the Kurio.Server browser-integration endpoint — start with link capture only (no popup UI) as a first GitHub issue

Introduce a dedicated 'monitor' layer in Kurio.Core (an IDownloadMonitor-style read-only projection over DownloadJob/DownloadQueue state) that Kurio.Server's SignalR hub subscribes to, instead of the hub reading engine internals directly — keeps the engine ignorant of transport/broadcast concerns

Adopt write-temp-then-atomic-rename for all JSON state persistence in Kurio.Core (metadata files and segment/part-progress files) to guarantee resume integrity across crashes/power loss; audit current JSON persistence code for this pattern

Split resume-progress data into a separate per-download 'parts' file from the per-download 'metadata' file (mirroring DownloadListFileStorage vs PartListFileStorage) so segment/range state can be rewritten frequently without rewriting slower-changing metadata
Support multiple independent, schedulable download queues (not just a single global queue) with a small reserved ID range for built-in queues, exposed via both the REST API and the Blazor dashboard

Add typed resume-failure exceptions (e.g. RemoteResourceChangedException, ResumeSupportChangedException) to Kurio.Core so pause/resume logic can explicitly distinguish 'safe to resume via Range' from 'must restart download' rather than treating all resume failures generically
Consider sparse-file pre-allocation for large downloads (abstracted per-OS) instead of writing zero-filled placeholder files, to reduce disk I/O and speed up initial allocation

File a backlog issue for first-class HLS/m3u8 (streaming media) download support in Kurio.Core designed against the same DownloadJob/Queue abstractions used for HTTP, as a stepping stone toward the yt-dlp integration already in Kurio's backlog

name: pyLoad
popularity: ~6-7k GitHub stars, actively maintained (rewritten for Python 3 as 'pyload-ng', continuous releases on PyPI/Docker); long-running project (since ~2009)
architecture: Single long-running Python process (module/Core.py historically, now pyload package) hosting a central Core object that owns manager singletons: PluginManager, HookManager (now AddonManager), AccountManager, ThreadManager, FileManager/DatabaseBackend (SQLite). Downloads are represented as PyFile objects grouped into PyPackage objects; state (package/link list, status, position, per-file progress) is persisted in a SQLite DB rather than flat files, so resume after crash means reloading package/link rows and re-querying the hoster plugin for a fresh direct-download URL (pyLoad does not persist raw HTTP byte-range state itself — the underlying chunked downloader writes `.chunk` temp files and a `.hash`/info file per download that let it resume within a session, and hoster plugins are responsible for re-authenticating/re-resolving links after restart). A web interface (Flask-based in pyload-ng) and JSON/RPC-style API (`Api` class, callable via HTTP, exposed with `@Expose` decorators) is the only client; no separate desktop GUI ships. Everything (web UI, CLI, RPC clients) talks to the same in-process Api object over an HTTP+JSON bridge.
standout_features: Four distinct plugin base classes with regex-based dispatch: Hoster (implements process() to resolve+download one link), Crypter/Decrypter (implements decrypt(), appends discovered packages/links to self.packages as (name, urls, folder) tuples so link decryption can recursively expand one URL into many), Account (login/premium-status/traffic-quota plugins keyed by hoster domain), and Hook/Addon (singleton, event-driven, full Api access, used for things like UpdateManager, ExtractArchive, CaptchaTrader)

URL-to-plugin matching is purely a compiled __pattern__ regex per plugin; the PluginManager scans all installed plugin patterns against each submitted URL to pick a handler — a simple, hot-swappable plugin discovery mechanism (new hoster support = drop in one .py file matching a regex)

Captcha handling is abstracted through self.decryptCaptcha(url, ...) on the base Plugin class, which hands the captcha image off to either connected web/GUI clients (interactive solve) or to a Hook plugin (e.g. a paid solver service) implementing an event-map hook (newCaptchaTask/captchaCorrect callbacks) — decoupling captcha solving strategy from hoster plugin logic entirely

Hooks register for lifecycle events either by overriding named methods (coreReady, downloadFinished(pyfile), downloadStarts, etc.) or via an event_map dict of event-name -> method-name, giving a lightweight pub/sub system without a full event bus dependency

Account plugins are looked up dynamically per-download via self.account = pyfile.m.core.accountManager.getAccountPlugin(name) so a hoster plugin can opt into using stored premium credentials transparently
pitfalls_to_avoid: pyLoad's original codebase went years without a Python-3-compatible stable release, causing ecosystem fragmentation (multiple abandoned forks); avoid designing Kurio around a single aging engine version, keep Kurio.Core independent of API/UI framework churn

Regex-only plugin dispatch became a maintenance burden as hosters changed URL schemes constantly, requiring frequent plugin updates just to keep parity — a lesson to keep protocol/site-specific logic in swappable, independently-versioned plugin assemblies rather than baked into the core engine

Captcha/premium-account plugin ecosystem decayed because many required paid solver services or reverse-engineered login flows that broke silently; monitor for a similar problem if Kurio ever adds site-specific extractors
ideas_for_kurio: Define a Kurio.Plugins.Abstractions assembly with an IHostHandler/ICrawler interface (a UrlPattern property + ResolveAsync returning one-or-more direct download descriptors) so future protocol/site support (FTP, streaming extractors, redirector sites) can be added as separate NuGet-loaded plugins rather than editing Kurio.Core

Add an IAccountProvider abstraction (stored per-host credentials + premium/traffic-quota state) surfaced through the REST API/dashboard so future premium-hoster or authenticated-download support has a slot to plug into without redesigning DownloadTask

Add a pluggable ICaptchaChallengeHandler pipeline: engine raises a 'challenge required' event over SignalR, Blazor dashboard renders the challenge image/interactive prompt, user response flows back through the hub to unblock the download — mirrors pyLoad's decouple-solving-from-download-logic pattern and is directly usable for any future auth-walled hoster support

Adopt an event_map-style lightweight event registration on Kurio.Core's engine (C# events/delegates keyed by name: OnDownloadStarted, OnDownloadFinished, OnQueueChanged) so a future plugin/extension system (per backlog) can subscribe without subclassing core engine types

Consider persisting queue/package state in SQLite (via EF Core) instead of/alongside JSON files once queue sizes grow — gives crash-safe partial updates and easy querying for the dashboard, addressing a gap JSON-file persistence has at scale

name: JDownloader 2 / MyJDownloader remote API
repo: mirror/jdownloader (unofficial GitHub mirror of the closed-source JDownloader 2 codebase); official remote API at api.jdownloader.org
popularity: JDownloader itself has millions of users; the GitHub mirror has a few hundred stars and is a community-maintained mirror, not the official repo (source is closed, distributed via appjaredupdate); MyJDownloader wrapper libraries (Python myjdapi, C# My.JDownloader.Api) each have modest star counts (dozens-hundreds) but are actively used/maintained as the de facto integration path
language: Java (client), REST/JSON over HTTPS (MyJDownloader API), wrapper libs in Python/C#/others
architecture: JDownloader is a thick Java desktop client with its own embedded plugin engine (LinkGrabber for crawling/decrypting, DownloadWatchdog for the download queue, LinkCollector for pre-download link management). Remote control does not use a server pushing to clients directly — instead the JD client establishes an outbound long-poll/HTTPS connection to a central relay (api.jdownloader.org), registers itself as a 'device' under a MyJDownloader account, and remote clients (phone apps, web UI, third-party scripts) authenticate against the same relay, discover the device, and submit RPC 'actions' that get queued and delivered to the device on its next poll — this NAT/firewall-traversing polling-relay model is the core design differentiator from a typical client-server API.
standout_features: End-to-end encrypted RPC: session established via login handshake deriving an AES-128-CBC key + HMAC-SHA256 signing key from the user's email/password (via a server-secret + client-secret split), so the relay operator (or a MITM) cannot read RPC payloads or device responses — every request/response body is encrypted and signed, not just transport-layer TLS

RPC surface organized into clear namespaces mapping to JD's internal managers: LinkGrabberV2 (addLinks, queryLinks/queryPackages for the pre-download crawl queue, moveToDownloadlist, renameLink), DownloadsV2 (queryLinks/queryPackages for the active download queue, cleanup, rename, setEnabled), DownloadController (start/stop/pause, getSpeedInBps, getState), Accounts (add/list/enable premium accounts), System/Jd (restart, shutdown, exitJd, getStorageInfo), Config (get/set/query arbitrary plugin settings) — i.e. the RPC API is a thin typed wrapper over the same manager objects the desktop GUI itself calls

Two-stage link pipeline (LinkGrabber staging queue -> Downloader queue) lets decrypter/crawler plugins expand a single pasted URL (e.g. a container or folder link) into many resolved direct links for user review/dedup before they're committed to the actual download queue — separates 'discovery' from 'commit to download'

Device-offline tolerance: because commands are relayed through polling rather than a direct socket, remote clients can queue actions (add links, start downloads) even while the desktop client is asleep/offline, and they get delivered/executed once it reconnects — a robustness property worth having for any mobile-remote-control feature

Decrypter/crawler plugins are entirely separate from hoster/downloader plugins (see src/jd/plugins/decrypter/*), so 'figure out what real file URLs a folder/share page points to' is cleanly decoupled from 'download this direct file URL with resume support'
pitfalls_to_avoid: Relying on a third-party-operated relay (api.jdownloader.org) for all remote control is a single point of failure/privacy concern outside the user's control — worth avoiding for Kurio; SignalR direct to Kurio.Server (self-hosted) sidesteps this entirely, which is already the better design

JDownloader's plugin/source code is closed and distributed as signed, auto-updating jars pulled from JD's own CDN — this made the community mirror lag official releases and blocks true open contribution; Kurio should keep its plugin contract open/versioned in a public NuGet feed instead

The two-queue (linkgrabber vs download list) model adds UX complexity that confuses many users about 'why isn't my link downloading yet' — if Kurio adopts a discovery/crawl step for future site plugins, make the staging step optional/auto-commit for the common single-direct-link case rather than always forcing a review step
ideas_for_kurio: Add an offline-tolerant command queue on Kurio.Server: SignalR hub commands (AddDownload, Pause, Resume) issued while a client is disconnected get persisted server-side and replayed/acknowledged on reconnect, rather than requiring the Blazor client to be live — useful groundwork for a future mobile/remote-control app

Introduce a two-stage 'link discovery' queue distinct from the active download queue: an ILinkCrawler plugin can expand one submitted URL (folder/share page, playlist) into N resolved DownloadRequest entries that land in a review list before the user commits them to Kurio.Core's download queue — directly enables future yt-dlp/streaming and decrypter-style plugin support from the backlog

Design the future plugin RPC/extension surface as namespaced command groups mirroring engine managers (Queue.*, Speed.*, Accounts.*, Config.*) exposed identically over both the REST API and SignalR hub, so third-party integrations (mobile app, browser extension) get one consistent typed contract instead of ad hoc endpoints

For the backlog's 'browser integration / clipboard link capture' item, mirror MyJDownloader's device-registration model: give Kurio.Server a lightweight pairing flow (short-lived pairing code) so a browser extension or clipboard watcher can register as a trusted 'device' and push AddDownload commands without needing a full user login each time

If premium/authenticated hoster support is ever added, adopt JD's Accounts namespace pattern (per-host credential store + enable/disable + traffic/premium status query) exposed as its own REST/SignalR surface, separate from the download-task model

name: Persepolis Download Manager
popularity: ~7,400 stars, actively maintained (last push Oct 2025), 315 open issues, multi-platform maintainers for Linux/BSD/macOS/Windows
architecture: Single Python process: a Qt (PySide6/PyQt5) GUI (persepolis/gui) driving a scripts package (persepolis/scripts) that used to be a thin wrapper over aria2's XML-RPC but has since replaced that with its own 'persepolis_lib' built on the Python requests library (avoids aria2 crashing mid-session). All state (not just a resume file) lives in three SQLite databases opened via data_base.py: a persistent persepolis.db with category_db_table, download_db_table (gid PRIMARY KEY, file_name, size, downloaded_size, connections, rate, eta, first/last_try_date, category FK), addlink_db_table (per-download options: proxy, auth, headers, cookies, connections, limit_value, start_time/end_time, after_download), and video_finder tables for yt-dlp based media grabs (video_gid/audio_gid pairs to be muxed); plus a temp_db (in-memory) for live per-session state and a plugins_db for queued links coming from the browser extension. Each 'category' acts as an independent queue: a QThread subclass (scripts/queue.py) polls the DB, honors a start_time/end_time window, and runs an 'after' action (shutdown, sleep, etc.) once the queue drains; it retries the whole category up to 5 times per cycle to catch newly queued/failed items. Browser integration (browser_integration.py) is a standard Chrome/Firefox Native Messaging host: it installs a JSON manifest plus a generated shell/registry-pointed intermediary script (persepolis_run_shell) that native messaging invokes with the actual link/cookie payload, writing into the plugins_db table that the main app polls.
standout_features: Per-category queue = independent scheduler thread with its own start/end time window and post-completion action (shutdown/sleep/close app), not just a single global scheduler

SQLite (three separate DBs: main config/downloads, in-memory temp/live-state, and a plugins queue) instead of a flat JSON resume file — gives crash-safe, queryable state and clean separation of 'durable settings' vs 'live ephemeral progress'
Dropped aria2 XML-RPC dependency over time in favor of an in-process Python download engine (persepolis_lib) to avoid RPC-crash reliability issues
Native-messaging browser integration installs a tiny generated wrapper script/registry key per browser rather than hardcoding paths, so it survives app relocation
Built-in yt-dlp wrapper with separate video/audio gid tracking and a muxing step once both finish
ideas_for_kurio: Add a Queue entity independent of the global engine: each queue has its own optional time window (start/end) and an 'on completion' action (shutdown host, notify, run script) — model as a QueueSchedule value object with StartTimeOfDay/EndTimeOfDay/DaysOfWeek plus AfterQueueAction enum, evaluated by a background IHostedService

Consider splitting Kurio.Core's JSON state persistence into 'durable config' vs 'live progress' concerns even if staying JSON-based (e.g. a lightweight SQLite or LiteDB store for the download catalog/categories, separate from an in-memory progress broadcaster) to reduce write amplification during active transfers

For a future browser integration issue, register a standard Native Messaging host manifest (per browser) pointing at a tiny wrapper executable, rather than requiring the extension to know Kurio's absolute install path
For streaming/yt-dlp support, track video-only and audio-only download IDs as a linked pair with a 'muxing pending' status so the queue UI can show one composite item until ffmpeg merges them
pitfalls_to_avoid: Its scheduler re-scans the whole category for retries in a fixed loop of 5 iterations — a time-boxed hack; prefer an event-driven queue re-evaluation instead of a hardcoded retry-count loop

Direct aria2 XML-RPC integration caused reliability problems (aria2 process crashes taking down RPC session) — if Kurio ever wraps an external engine like aria2, isolate it behind a supervised child process with restart/reconnect logic rather than assuming a stable long-lived RPC channel

name: uGet
popularity: ~151 stars, explicitly marked 'not under active development' by maintainers, last push Oct 2024, 69 open issues — effectively dormant/reference-only
architecture: Native GTK app (uget-gtk) over a core library (uglib) that defines a formal plugin ABI: UgPluginInterface is a C vtable (global_init/global_finalize/global_set/global_get for process-wide setup, and per-instance init/finalize/set_state/get_state/set/get for each download) registered via ug_plugin_interface_register and looked up by name or by URL scheme/file-type prefix ('scheme.' or 'file.'). Each active download is a UgPlugin instance with its own message queue (ug_plugin_post/ug_plugin_pop_all) so the GTK UI thread polls plugins asynchronously instead of blocking; built-in plugins are UgPlugin-curl (HTTP/FTP via libcurl) and UgPlugin-aria2 (spawns/talks to aria2 over XML-RPC for BitTorrent/Metalink/multi-source). Categories (UgCategory) are queues with active_limit/finished_limit/recycled_limit knobs controlling how many downloads run concurrently and how much finished/trashed history is retained. Persistent state is saved through a UgData/UgMarkup interface (custom XML-like markup serialization implemented per struct) rather than JSON or SQLite. Scheduling is a UgScheduleForm: a 7×24 boolean grid (day-of-week x hour) plus a global speed cap, letting users paint which hours/days downloading is throttled or disabled.
standout_features: Clean C vtable plugin ABI (UgPluginInterface) separating global (process) lifecycle from per-download instance lifecycle, with plugins matched by name OR by URL scheme/file-type — a template for a backend-agnostic download engine abstraction
Per-plugin async message queue (post/pop_all) decouples the UI polling loop from engine internals
Category = queue with three independent limits: concurrently-active, kept-finished, and kept-in-recycle-bin counts
7x24 weekly grid UI for schedule-based speed throttling (paint which hour-of-day/day-of-week gets a lower cap) instead of a single start/end time window
Delegates BitTorrent/Metalink/multi-source entirely to aria2 via XML-RPC as an optional plugin, keeping the native curl plugin simple for plain HTTP/FTP
ideas_for_kurio: Define an IDownloadEngine (or IDownloadBackend) abstraction with clearly separated static/global capability metadata (supported schemes/file types, one-time init) vs per-download instance operations (Start/Pause/Resume/Cancel/GetState/SetSpeedLimit), so alternative backends (e.g. an optional aria2-RPC backend from the existing backlog item) can be registered and selected by URL scheme without touching the core engine

Add per-category (per-queue) limits beyond just 'max concurrent active downloads': also a 'max retained completed history' and 'max retained failed/recycled items' count, exposed as settings on the queue entity

For speed-limit UX, offer an optional weekly 7x24 grid (day x hour) editor in the Blazor dashboard as an alternative to a single daily time-window, letting users define e.g. 'throttle 9am-6pm on weekdays, unrestricted otherwise' visually

Keep the async message-queue pattern already implicit in SignalR broadcasting, but make sure Kurio.Core exposes it as decoupled progress events per download rather than requiring the caller to poll each engine instance
pitfalls_to_avoid: uGet's custom UgMarkup serialization format is bespoke and now unmaintained tech debt with no ecosystem tooling — Kurio's existing plain-JSON state persistence is the better choice; don't reinvent a proprietary text format

Project is effectively abandoned partly because the aria2-XML-RPC coupling made the app fragile to external process lifecycle (matches Persepolis's experience) — treat any external engine integration as an optional, sandboxed plugin, never a hard dependency of core

name: Xtreme Download Manager (XDM)
language: C# (.NET, targeting both .NET Framework/legacy and modern .NET via shared XDM.Core; separate WinForms/WPF UI for Windows and GTK UI for Linux)
popularity: ~7,900 stars, large open-issue backlog (~850), last push Jan 2024 — very popular but slowing maintenance cadence
architecture: A single desktop process (per-OS UI project: XDM.WinForms.IntegrationUI/XDM.Wpf.UI on Windows, XDM.Gtk.UI on Linux) hosts a shared XDM.Core engine. Segmented downloads are modeled as Chunk objects (Uri, Offset, Size, Downloaded, ChunkState: Ready/InProgress/FailedTransient/FailedFatal/Finished) under Downloader/Progressive (plain HTTP range-based multi-connection) and Downloader/Adaptive (Hls/Dash) for streaming formats, plus a YDLWrapper for yt-dlp-backed sites. Persistence is SQLite (System.Data.SQLite) via DataAccess/AppDB with a WITHOUT ROWID 'downloads' table keyed by a string id, storing all download metadata (status, progress, proxy, auth, target dir); queues are a separate binary-serialized DownloadQueue (versioned via QueueSerializerV1: id, name, list of download ids, optional DownloadSchedule with StartTime/EndTime ticks + a Days-of-week bitmask) persisted outside the DB. A Scheduler class runs a 60-second Timer comparing current hour:minute against each queue's schedule to start/stop its downloads. Browser integration is the most notable subsystem: rather than classic Native Messaging, XDM.Core.BrowserMonitoring.IpcHttpMessageProcessor runs a tiny loopback-only HTTP server (NanoServer bound to 127.0.0.1:8597) that a Manifest V3 browser extension (webRequest permission, service-worker background script) talks to over plain HTTP POST — routes include /sync (poll current filter config + pending video list as JSON), /download and /link (single/batch capture), /media and /vid (candidate media stream detected / user-selected video to grab), /tab-update (tab title/URL for naming), /clear, and /args. The extension's RequestWatcher listens to chrome.webRequest (onSendHeaders/onHeadersReceived/onErrorOccurred), matches each request against server-supplied filter rules (blockedHosts, fileExts, mediaExts, matchingHosts like 'googlevideo', mediaTypes, regex urlPatterns) fetched via /sync, and POSTs matches to the app. VideoUrlHelper on the app side further classifies HLS (.m3u8) vs DASH (.mpd) vs YouTube's own format manifests vs generic progressive video by Content-Type/size threshold, and de-dupes by tracking which tabs already resolved to an HLS/DASH manifest (m3u8MpdTabs) and which URLs look like fragmented mp4 init segments (suspectedMp4Fragments) to avoid re-capturing every media fragment as a separate 'video'. A legacy Windows Named-Pipe based NativeMessagingHostHandler (PipeName 'XDM_Ipc_Browser_Monitoring_Pipe') and an even older raw Native Messaging stdio handler exist in the codebase but are effectively superseded/commented out in favor of the loopback HTTP approach.
standout_features: Ditched Chrome Native Messaging (stdio JSON framing + per-browser manifest installation) in favor of a simple loopback-only HTTP server the extension calls directly — much less install/registry friction, still not exposed off localhost

Extension-side request filtering rules (blocked hosts, extensions, content-types, regex URL patterns, 'matching hosts' like googlevideo) are server-configured and pulled by the extension via /sync, so filter logic lives in one place (the app) and can change without shipping a new extension version

Media-type disambiguation pipeline: Content-Type + URL pattern checks for HLS/DASH/YouTube-manifest formats, size-threshold gating for 'is this really a video worth offering', and de-dupe heuristics (skip normal-video capture on tabs that already resolved an HLS/DASH manifest; skip likely fragmented-mp4 init segments) to avoid flooding the user with false video-capture prompts
Queues are versioned, binary-serialized objects independent from the SQLite download table, with a day-of-week bitmask + start/end time for weekly recurring schedules

Shared cross-platform C# core (XDM.Core) driving distinct native UIs per OS (WinForms/WPF vs GTK) — closest architectural analog to a hypothetical Kurio engine/UI split, though Kurio's split (Core engine + separate Server/Web) is already cleaner
ideas_for_kurio: Open a GitHub issue for 'browser link/media capture via companion extension': add a loopback-only HTTP endpoint set to Kurio.Server (e.g. under /api/capture) with routes mirroring /sync (push current filter config: blocked hosts, file/media extensions, url regex patterns), /link (single or batch captured request → enqueue download), and /media (candidate streaming media detected) — avoids the Native Messaging manifest-per-browser installation entirely and fits naturally since Kurio.Server already exposes a REST API

Ship a minimal MV3 browser extension (manifest permissions: webRequest, downloads, tabs, storage, host_permissions *://*/*) whose background service worker watches chrome.webRequest events, filters by extension/content-type/regex fetched from Kurio.Server's /sync, and POSTs matches — bind the extension's target host/port to Kurio.Server's own address so it works whether Kurio.Server runs locally or on a LAN box

For streaming media capture, replicate the classification pipeline: check Content-Type for HLS(m3u8)/DASH(mpd) vs generic video, apply a minimum-size threshold config, and track 'has this tab already resolved a manifest' to suppress duplicate fragment-level capture noise — surface this as a MediaCaptureOptions section in Kurio.Core config

Model queues as first-class objects separate from individual downloads (a DownloadQueue with Id, Name, ordered list of DownloadIds, optional weekly Schedule with Days-of-week bitmask) so scheduling and 'shutdown after queue completes' can be added later without redesigning the download entity itself

For the resume/state format, keep Kurio's existing JSON persistence but consider XDM's SQLite 'downloads' table pattern (WITHOUT ROWID, string primary key = download GUID) as a fallback design if JSON-file-per-download proves to not scale well with hundreds of queued items
pitfalls_to_avoid: XDM's Scheduler polls once per 60-second Timer tick and matches on exact hour:minute equality to fire start/stop — if the app is asleep, paused, or the timer tick is delayed past the exact minute, the scheduled action can be silently skipped entirely; use a range check (now >= start && now < end, evaluated on every tick) rather than exact-match triggers

The codebase carries three generations of browser-IPC mechanisms side by side (raw stdio Native Messaging, Windows Named Pipes, and the current loopback HTTP server) with large commented-out blocks left in place — decide on one browser-integration transport for Kurio up front and don't leave dead alternatives in the tree

Binding the capture/browser-IPC HTTP listener to loopback only is essential (XDM does this correctly on 127.0.0.1:8597); if Kurio's REST API already binds to all interfaces for LAN dashboard access, the capture endpoints must be scoped/authenticated separately so a hostile webpage can't drive an internet-exposed Kurio.Server instance via CORS-less POSTs from the browser extension context

name: Varia
language: Python (GTK4/GObject, PyGObject) + Deno (browser extension helper) + C/Vala build via Meson
popularity: ~1.8k stars, 99 forks, 507 commits; actively developed (has a 'next' branch), Flathub-first distribution, Windows/macOS support experimental
architecture: Varia is a thin GTK4/Libadwaita frontend, not an engine of its own: on startup it spawns `aria2c` as a background subprocess (see src/download and variamain.py) and talks to it exclusively through the aria2 JSON-RPC interface, wrapped by the Python `aria2p` client library rather than raw JSON-RPC calls. A dedicated background thread (`listen_to_aria2()`) polls aria2's `tellActive`/`tellWaiting`/`tellStopped`-style status endpoints on an interval and marshals updates back to the GTK main loop to refresh rows in the download list (poll-based, not push/streaming). Torrents/magnet links are handed to the same aria2 instance (libtorrent-backed). Video/audio URLs take a separate code path: yt-dlp is invoked as its own subprocess for extraction/format-selection before the resulting direct URL (or yt-dlp's own segmented download) is handed off; FFmpeg is used for post-processing/muxing. A companion browser extension ('Varia Integrator', built with Deno tooling) captures links from Firefox/Chrome and forwards them to the desktop app's local server.py (a small local HTTP/RPC endpoint) so 'send to Varia' works from the browser. Session resume relies on aria2's own on-disk `.aria2` control files plus persisted GIDs so the app can reattach to in-progress transfers after restart.
standout_features: Delegates all transport complexity (multi-connection HTTP, torrent, resume) to aria2 via aria2p, keeping the GTK app a pure UI+orchestration layer
Unified queue that mixes plain HTTP downloads, torrents, and yt-dlp media jobs in one list with distinct row renderers
Local HTTP server (server.py) exposing an add-download endpoint that the browser extension posts to, enabling 'right click -> download with Varia' from any tab
Single global bandwidth limit plus authentication (basic auth) fields exposed per-download, mapped straight onto aria2 RPC options
Notification handler module decoupled from the main window (notification_handler.py) for completion/error toasts
ideas_for_kurio: Add a lightweight local HTTP endpoint on Kurio.Server (e.g. POST /api/downloads/capture) purpose-built for a future browser extension to push right-click 'Download with Kurio' links, mirroring Varia's Integrator pattern

Model yt-dlp/streaming support as a separate DownloadKind in Kurio.Core (distinct from the HTTP segmented engine) so it can shell out to yt-dlp and report progress through the same SignalR progress hub without forcing streaming downloads through the byte-range/segment code path

Consider whether an aria2-integration mode (spawn aria2c, drive it over JSON-RPC) is worth offering as an alternative backend for protocols Kurio.Core doesn't natively support (e.g. torrents/FTP) rather than reimplementing them
Expose a single global speed-limit plus optional per-download override in the dashboard UI, matching the simple mental model users expect from aria2-style managers
pitfalls_to_avoid: Polling-thread-based progress updates (Varia's listen_to_aria2) are simpler than a push model but add latency and busy-work; Kurio already has SignalR push, so keep leveraging that instead of introducing polling

Tight coupling to a single external engine (aria2) makes platform packaging heavy (bundling aria2c/yt-dlp/ffmpeg per OS); if Kurio adds yt-dlp support, plan explicit binary-provisioning/update strategy up front

name: Parabolic
language: C# / .NET 10 (libparabolic core) with native GNOME (GTK4/libadwaita, C++ via GTK bindings) and WinUI front ends
popularity: ~6.9k stars, 85 open issues, active development (recent issues from 2026 about yt-dlp auth diagnostics); actively maintained flagship Nickvision app
architecture: Follows an MVC-ish split: 'Nickvision.Parabolic.Shared' is the platform-agnostic core (Models/Controllers/Services/Events/Helpers) referenced by both the GNOME and WinUI head projects, which supply only views. Models directory shows the domain: Download.cs, DownloadOptions.cs, DownloadStatus.cs, Media.cs/MediaSelectionItem.cs/Format.cs (yt-dlp's probed format list), HistoricDownload.cs/RecoverableDownload.cs (persisted download history / crash-recovery), PostProcessor.cs/PostProcessorArgument.cs (ffmpeg post-processing steps), Executable.cs (locating/validating yt-dlp, ffmpeg, aria2c binaries), YtdlpException.cs (structured error mapping from yt-dlp's stderr/exit codes). Controllers (AddDownloadDialogController, MainWindowController, HistoryViewController) mediate between UI events and the Services layer, which wraps yt-dlp/ffmpeg/aria2c as supervised subprocesses, parses their stdout progress lines into strongly-typed progress events, and optionally offloads the actual transfer to aria2c (aria2c can be selected as yt-dlp's --downloader for improved multi-connection throughput). Crash/interruption recovery is handled via RecoverableDownload records that let a download resume post-crash by replaying yt-dlp/ffmpeg with recorded options rather than a raw byte-offset resume.
standout_features: Clean core-library/UI separation (libparabolic-equivalent 'Shared' project) shared across two completely different native UI stacks (GTK4/libadwaita and WinUI) -- a direct model for splitting Kurio.Core from any future desktop shell
Executable.cs abstraction for discovering/validating bundled vs. system yt-dlp/ffmpeg/aria2c binaries with version checks
Optional aria2c as yt-dlp's downloader backend for parallel-connection speed on plain HTTP media, while yt-dlp itself remains the extractor/muxer
Structured YtdlpException mapping known yt-dlp failure signatures (auth required, bot check, geo-block) into typed, actionable UI errors rather than raw stderr dumps
Persisted download History with 'HistoryLength' retention setting and RecoverableDownload state to resume/re-run interrupted downloads after an app crash
Browser extension (extension/ dir) for Firefox/Chrome to send video URLs to the desktop app, similar to Varia's Integrator
ideas_for_kurio: Adopt Parabolic's Executable-discovery pattern for Kurio: an IExternalToolLocator service that finds/validates yt-dlp and ffmpeg (bundled or system PATH), surfaced via a Kurio.Server health/settings endpoint the Blazor dashboard can show ('yt-dlp: v2026.x found / missing')

Add a typed exception/error-mapping layer for any embedded yt-dlp process (parse known failure substrings from stderr) and surface them as structured DownloadError DTOs over SignalR instead of raw process output

Introduce a RecoverableDownload-style persisted record: if Kurio.Server crashes/restarts mid-download of a yt-dlp job, store enough state (URL, format id, output path, post-processor args) to safely re-invoke rather than trying byte-range resume on a process-based download

Model format/quality selection as a two-step flow like Parabolic's AddDownloadDialogController: probe (yt-dlp -J) to list available Media/Format options, let the user pick resolution/codec/audio-only, then enqueue -- expose this as a POST /api/downloads/probe + POST /api/downloads endpoint pair
Consider a small browser extension later (mirrors Parabolic's extension/) that just posts a URL to Kurio.Server's capture endpoint, deferring all format logic to the server
pitfalls_to_avoid: Don't conflate yt-dlp-driven downloads with the segmented HTTP engine's pause/resume semantics -- they need separate progress-reporting and resume strategies (process replay vs byte offset)

Structured error mapping from a rapidly-changing external tool (yt-dlp) is high-maintenance; keep the mapping table small/pattern-based and fail open to a generic error rather than trying to enumerate every yt-dlp failure mode

name: DownThemAll! (WebExtension)
language: TypeScript (WebExtension: background scripts + HTML-based windows), webpack build
popularity: ~1.1k stars, 126 forks, 459 commits on master; actively maintained but self-described as functionally reduced vs. the legacy XUL add-on due to WebExtension API limits
architecture: Manifest V2 WebExtension with a persistent background script (lib/background.ts) that owns a Manager (lib/manager/man.ts) coordinating a queue of Download objects (lib/manager/download.ts, extending BaseDownload). Because WebExtensions cannot implement their own network stack, actual byte transfer is delegated entirely to the browser's native `browser.downloads` API (lib/browser.ts) -- DTA's value-add is everything around that: mass link/image discovery in a page (lib/select.ts, lib/textlinks.ts), regex/glob filtering (lib/filters.ts implements a Matcher that accepts literal strings, `*`/`?` fnmatch globs, or `/regex/flags` syntax, consolidating multiple filters into merged sensitive/insensitive RegExp pairs for fast bulk matching), per-domain concurrency Limits (lib/manager/limits.ts, a Prefs-backed map of domain -> max concurrent downloads, default global concurrency 4), a Renamer (lib/manager/renamer.ts) implementing the classic '*name*.*ext*' mask-substitution language for batch file naming, a Preroller (lib/manager/preroller.ts) that HEAD-probes URLs before queuing to resolve filename/size/conflict, and a Scheduler (lib/manager/scheduler.ts) for queue ordering. Persistence is IndexedDB (lib/db.ts, database 'downloads', object store 'queue' keyed by autoincrement dbId with a by_position index) -- on save, RUNNING/RETRYING items are normalized back to QUEUED so a reload always resumes as queued rather than claiming to be actively running. Import/export of batches is handled by lib/imex.ts and lib/batches.ts (turns a list of discovered links into a reusable named batch template). windowstatetracker.ts persists window geometry across sessions.
standout_features: Mask-based batch renaming language (Renamer) letting users template output filenames from URL components, page title, counters, etc. across an entire batch

Filter Matcher supporting three input syntaxes (plain substring, glob with * and ?, and full /regex/flags) merged into a small number of consolidated RegExp objects for O(1)-ish bulk filtering of thousands of links
Per-domain concurrency limits map (not just one global concurrency slider) so e.g. a slow file host can be capped independently of the global setting
Preroller: proactively HEAD/GET-probes each queued URL to resolve real filename/extension/size and detect naming conflicts before the download actually starts
IndexedDB-backed queue persistence with defensive state-normalization on save (RUNNING -> QUEUED) so a browser restart never lies about a download's real state
Batches: named, reusable templates of a filtered/selected link set for repeatable mass-download workflows
ideas_for_kurio: Port the Renamer mask-template concept to Kurio: let users define an output filename/path template (e.g. `{host}/{date}/{filename}`) applied when adding batches of URLs, exposed as a field on the batch-add API

Add a Filters concept to Kurio's batch-add flow: accept a list of URLs plus an include/exclude filter (glob, regex, or plain substring) and only enqueue matches -- directly reusable in a future browser-extension-driven 'send all links matching X' feature

Add per-host/per-domain concurrency and speed-limit overrides in Kurio.Core (a Limits-style domain->maxConcurrent map) layered on top of the existing global speed limiter, configurable from the dashboard

Adopt a Preroller step in Kurio's add-download flow: before creating a Download entity, issue a HEAD request to resolve real filename (Content-Disposition), size, and range support, and flag naming conflicts up front instead of discovering them mid-transfer

For state persistence, follow DTA's defensive normalization rule: on any snapshot/save of Kurio's JSON state file, downgrade any 'InProgress' download to 'Queued' so a server crash never leaves a download claiming to be actively transferring when it isn't
Add a Batches feature: let users save a named, filtered set of URLs (e.g. from a pasted list) as a reusable template they can re-run, mirroring DTA's imex.ts/batches.ts
pitfalls_to_avoid: DTA's architecture is fundamentally constrained by delegating transfer to `browser.downloads` -- it cannot do true segmented multi-connection downloads or resume-from-arbitrary-offset; Kurio's Core engine already avoids this limitation by owning the HTTP transfer, so don't regress toward a 'thin UI over OS download manager' model

The regex/glob filter merging logic (consolidateRegexps) is a nice perf trick but adds real complexity (separate sensitive/insensitive RegExp trees) -- if porting filters to Kurio, a much simpler linear list of compiled Regex plus early-exit is likely sufficient at .NET's expected scale

name: Downloader (bezzad/Downloader)
popularity: ~1,700 GitHub stars, 248 forks, actively maintained (0 open issues at time of check, CI across Windows/Linux/macOS, used by v2rayN which has 112k+ stars). MIT license, no external dependencies.
architecture: Client-side, in-process library (no server component) built around DownloadService as the orchestrator, DownloadConfiguration for tunable behavior, and DownloadPackage as a lightweight, JSON-serializable state snapshot (URL, file path, per-chunk byte ranges/positions — not the actual bytes). Files are split into ChunkCount segments; when ParallelDownload=true, each chunk runs as an independent HTTP range request and chunks write directly into their offset of the final file (no temp per-chunk files), requiring the server to support Content-Length/Accept-Ranges/Content-Range with fallback to single-stream if absent. Pause/Resume uses stream-level locking for instant suspend/continue; longer-lived resume works by retaining/serializing the DownloadPackage and re-passing it into DownloadFileTaskAsync(pack). EnableAutoResumeDownload appends the serialized package JSON to the tail of the in-progress '.download' file itself (self-contained sidecar-less resume state), read back on next attempt then truncated off once the file completes and is renamed to the target name.
standout_features: DownloadPackage as a small serializable resume token decoupled from file bytes, resumable either by explicit hand-off or by auto-detecting appended state in the .download temp file
Parallel range-request chunking that writes straight into final-file offsets, avoiding per-chunk temp files and a merge step
MaximumBytesPerSecond global throttle plus granular ChunkDownloadProgressChanged / DownloadProgressChanged events for per-segment and aggregate speed/ETA reporting
MaxTryAgainOnFailure + BlockTimeout give a simple built-in retry/backoff loop per chunk without needing an external resilience library
Fluent RequestConfiguration for headers/cookies/proxy/auth, and graceful fallback to non-parallel mode when the server doesn't advertise range support
ideas_for_kurio: Adopt the 'append serialized state to the temp file itself' auto-resume trick as an alternative/complement to Kurio's separate JSON state file — could reduce file-count clutter for large queues and guarantee state and partial bytes never get out of sync

Expose a Kurio.Core equivalent of ChunkDownloadProgressChanged over SignalR so the Blazor dashboard can render a per-segment progress bar (visualizing which byte ranges are done) instead of only an aggregate bar

Add automatic fallback path when a server lacks Accept-Ranges/Content-Range: detect via a HEAD/Range probe and degrade to single-connection sequential download rather than failing outright — check whether Kurio.Core already does this and add an explicit integration test for servers without range support

Consider explicitly guarding against BinaryFormatter for any legacy resume-state code path (Downloader's docs call out this security pitfall) — confirm Kurio's persistence uses System.Text.Json only, never BinaryFormatter

File this as a GitHub issue: 'Support resuming from a DownloadPackage-like token without requiring the original queue entry' to allow exporting/importing an individual paused download independent of full queue state

name: FluentFTP
popularity: ~3.4k GitHub stars, 3,555+ commits, MIT license. Actively maintained with regular contributions and Docker-based automated test suite against real FTP servers.
architecture: Pure-managed FTP/FTPS client library, no server or process component — designed to be embedded directly in an application via the FtpClient class. Fully async/await with CancellationToken support on all operations. Handles the full FTP command set (LIST parsing across many server dialects, permissions/CHMOD, hashing/checksums via HASH/XCRC/XMD5/XSHA commands where server-supported), SSL/TLS (including TLS 1.3 and client certs), and FXP (server-to-server transfers that never route bytes through the client). Proxy layer supports HTTP 1.1, SOCKS4/4a/5, User@Host, and BlueCoat proxy chaining. Security hardening explicitly guards against command injection, directory traversal, and malicious LIST-parser payloads.
standout_features: FXP support: transfer directly server-to-server without proxying bytes through the local machine — relevant if Kurio ever needs FTP-to-FTP or mirrored-source transfers
Automatic directory listing parsing across many divergent FTP server LIST formats (Unix, Windows/IIS, etc.) — a notoriously fragile area to hand-roll
Layered proxy abstraction (SOCKS4/4a/5, HTTP, User@Host, BlueCoat) that could be reused as a generic proxy-connection layer beyond just FTP
Explicit security posture against injection/traversal in a protocol that's historically been a source of client vulnerabilities
Async-first API with per-operation CancellationToken, matching modern .NET idioms that Kurio.Core already follows for HTTP
ideas_for_kurio: When implementing FTP support (open backlog item), take a dependency on FluentFTP rather than hand-rolling the protocol — its LIST-parsing and TLS/proxy layers are exactly the hard, unglamorous parts a small team shouldn't re-implement

Reuse FluentFTP's proxy type taxonomy (HTTP/SOCKS4/4a/5/User@Host) as the shape for Kurio's own 'proxy support' backlog item so one proxy configuration model can serve both HTTP(S) and future FTP downloads

File an issue: 'FTP download source via FluentFTP with segmented range-resume where server supports REST command' — note FTP resume is coarser (single REST offset, not N parallel chunks) so the Kurio.Core download-engine abstraction needs a resume strategy that can be either multi-range (HTTP) or single-offset (FTP)
If Kurio ever needs FXP-style mirrored transfers or an FTP-upload/publish feature, flag it as a stretch goal enabled almost for free by FluentFTP

name: MonoTorrent
popularity: ~1.2k GitHub stars, 409 forks, MIT license. Stable release 3.0.2 (Aug 2024); repository still active in 2026 (issues opened/updated as recently as April/July 2026) — moderately maintained, single primary maintainer.
architecture: Embeddable BitTorrent engine centered on a ClientEngine (process-wide connection/DHT/tracker manager) that hosts one or more TorrentManager instances (one per torrent), each exposing piece-picking, prioritization, and per-torrent rate limits, with ClientEngine additionally exposing overall/global rate limits. Persistence is via 'fast resume data' — a serialized snapshot of which pieces/blocks have been verified — that can be saved/restored to skip re-hashing the whole file set on restart, conceptually the direct BitTorrent analogue of Kurio's own JSON download-state persistence.
