Protocol coverage includes DHT (BEP 5), PEX (BEP 11), UDP/HTTP trackers, BitTorrent v2/hybrid torrents with merkle-layer piece hashing, IPv4/IPv6, and UPnP/NAT-PMP for automatic port mapping. It also ships a built-in tracker server implementation, so an app can act as tracker + client in one process. Piece selection is pluggable at the picker-strategy level (rarest-first as default, plus sequential and priority-aware pickers) rather than hardcoded.
standout_features: ClientEngine/TorrentManager two-level object model cleanly separating process-wide concerns (DHT, global rate limit, port mapping) from per-download concerns (piece picking, file priorities) — a good template for a multi-protocol download engine that needs both global and per-job settings
Fast-resume data as a purpose-built, non-full-rehash resume format — directly analogous to (and worth comparing against) whatever partial-download verification Kurio.Core does today
Pluggable piece-picker abstraction (rarest-first / sequential / priority) as a clean strategy-pattern example for swappable scheduling logic
Built-in overall + per-torrent bandwidth rate limiting API, i.e. rate limiting modeled as a first-class engine concept rather than bolted onto the transport layer
BitTorrent v2 hybrid-torrent and merkle-tree piece hashing support as a case study in incremental protocol versioning without breaking older clients
ideas_for_kurio: If/when torrent support ever gets reconsidered for the backlog, MonoTorrent is the only mature, actively-updated managed BitTorrent engine for .NET and should be the default choice over hand-rolling — but flag its single-maintainer risk profile before depending on it for anything core

Borrow the ClientEngine (global settings: bandwidth cap, port mapping, DHT) vs TorrentManager (per-job settings: priority, resume state) split as the mental model for Kurio.Core's own DownloadEngine vs per-download-job separation, since Kurio already needs global speed limits plus per-download state

Compare MonoTorrent's fast-resume-data approach against Kurio's current JSON state persistence to see if a similar 'verified-block bitmap' concept would make Kurio's segment-resume more robust against partial/corrupted chunk files after a crash
Consider UPnP/NAT-PMP port-mapping as a reusable pattern if Kurio ever adds any listen-for-inbound-connection feature (e.g. a P2P or LAN-transfer mode)

name: YoutubeDLSharp
language: C# (.NET, targets modern TFMs; wraps external yt-dlp/youtube-dl and ffmpeg binaries)
popularity: Actively maintained wrapper library, BSD-3-Clause license, widely used as the standard .NET yt-dlp binding; versions >=1.0 track yt-dlp specifically (0.x tracked legacy youtube-dl).
architecture: Not an in-process downloader at all — it's a process-management wrapper: the YoutubeDL high-level class exposes RunVideoDownload/RunAudioDownload/RunVideoPlaylistDownload/RunVideoDataFetch, each of which shells out to a yt-dlp (or ffmpeg) child process built via the lower-level YoutubeDLProcess class, which owns the actual Process object and exposes OutputReceived/ErrorReceived events for raw stdout/stderr line streaming (this is how progress percentages and diagnostic messages are captured/parsed). Configuration is via an OptionSet class whose properties map 1:1 to yt-dlp CLI flags (e.g. Format, RecodeVideo), and OptionSet configs can be persisted to files in the same format yt-dlp's native config files use, so settings are portable outside the wrapper too. Utils.DownloadYtDlp()/DownloadFFmpeg() self-bootstrap the required external binaries on first run. Progress is surfaced through the standard .NET IProgress<DownloadProgress> pattern with a percentage field, and all long operations take a CancellationToken.
standout_features: Self-updating/self-installing external binary bootstrap (Utils.DownloadYtDlp/DownloadFFmpeg) so the host app doesn't need to bundle or manually manage yt-dlp/ffmpeg versions

OptionSet property-per-CLI-flag design keeps the wrapper trivially up to date with new yt-dlp flags without needing new C# API surface for every option, and stays compatible with community yt-dlp config files
Clean two-tier API: high-level task methods (RunVideoDownload etc.) for common cases, low-level YoutubeDLProcess for raw process/stdout control when the wrapper's abstraction isn't enough
RunVideoDataFetch() separates metadata probing (title, formats, uploader) from the download decision, letting a caller present format-choice UI before committing to a download
Progress<T>/CancellationToken as the sole integration surface — no custom event-based API to learn beyond what .NET already provides
ideas_for_kurio: For the 'streaming media (yt-dlp)' backlog item, add a Kurio.Core.YtDlp adapter modeled directly on this: a process-supervisor class that shells to yt-dlp, parses its stdout progress lines, and republishes progress via the same IDownloadJob/SignalR progress contract used for HTTP(S) downloads so the Blazor dashboard doesn't need a special-cased UI for media downloads

Adopt the self-bootstrapping binary pattern (auto-download/pin a yt-dlp + ffmpeg version under Kurio's data directory, with a version-check/update path) as part of the future auto-update backlog item, rather than requiring the server operator to install yt-dlp manually

Model yt-dlp job configuration the same way OptionSet does — a typed options object whose properties mirror yt-dlp flags — so advanced users can pass through arbitrary yt-dlp options without Kurio.Server needing bespoke API surface for every option

Treat yt-dlp downloads as a distinct IDownloadJob type in Kurio.Core's queue (since they're process-driven, not HTTP-range-driven) but keep pause/resume semantics analogous: pause = suspend/kill process and persist the resumable URL+options, resume = re-invoke yt-dlp (most yt-dlp downloads aren't natively resumable mid-file the way HTTP range downloads are, so document this limitation explicitly in the design)

name: .NET IO/rate-limiting primitives (System.IO.Pipelines, System.Threading.RateLimiting, RandomAccess/SafeFileHandle)
language: C# / .NET (built into the runtime, .NET 6+ for RateLimiting/RandomAccess basics, refined through .NET 10)
popularity: First-party BCL components; System.Threading.RateLimiting ships as a standalone NuGet package (currently versioned 10.0.x) and is used inside ASP.NET Core's built-in rate-limiting middleware; System.IO.Pipelines powers Kestrel and SignalR internally, so it's battle-tested at massive scale.
architecture: Three complementary low-level primitives relevant to a segmented downloader: (1) System.IO.RandomAccess is a static class for thread-safe positional file I/O against a SafeFileHandle — Write/WriteAsync take an explicit byte offset and do not move/depend on a shared stream position, which is exactly what's needed for N parallel chunk-writers targeting disjoint byte ranges of the same file without a lock; RandomAccess.SetLength(handle, length) lets you preallocate the full file size up front (avoiding fragmentation and enabling out-of-order writes) instead of only appending sequentially via FileStream. (2) System.Threading.RateLimiting provides TokenBucketRateLimiter (plus FixedWindow/SlidingWindow/Concurrency limiters) as a reusable, testable token-bucket abstraction with TokenLimit/ReplenishmentPeriod/TokensPerPeriod/AutoReplenishment options — a drop-in replacement for a hand-rolled speed-limiter loop. (3) System.IO.Pipelines gives a zero-copy, backpressure-aware producer/consumer buffer abstraction (PipeReader/PipeWriter) designed for exactly the 'read from network socket, write to disk' streaming shape, avoiding repeated byte[] allocation/copy on the hot path.
standout_features: RandomAccess.Write/WriteAsync(SafeFileHandle, buffer, offset) is safe for concurrent multi-threaded writers to disjoint file regions with no explicit locking, unlike FileStream.Position which is inherently stateful and not concurrency-safe
RandomAccess.SetLength for upfront file preallocation, letting parallel chunk downloads begin writing at their target offset immediately instead of needing the file to already be 'grown' sequentially

TokenBucketRateLimiter as a standard, already-tested token-bucket implementation with clear knobs (TokenLimit, ReplenishmentPeriod, TokensPerPeriod) instead of a bespoke sleep/measure loop for bandwidth caps
System.IO.Pipelines' built-in backpressure so a fast network source can't blow up memory when the disk writer (or a throttled RateLimiter) is temporarily the bottleneck
All three are dependency-free BCL/first-party pieces, so adopting them adds no new third-party surface area — pure upgrade over hand-rolled equivalents
ideas_for_kurio: Replace any hand-rolled parallel-chunk file writing in Kurio.Core with RandomAccess.Write/WriteAsync against a single SafeFileHandle opened once per download, removing the need for per-chunk temp files or manual offset-seek-then-write sequences on FileStream

Use RandomAccess.SetLength to preallocate the destination file to its full Content-Length as soon as a download starts (when the server reports it), so segments can start writing to any offset immediately and disk fragmentation/growth stalls are reduced — file as a concrete issue: 'Preallocate file length via RandomAccess.SetLength before starting segmented download'

Swap Kurio.Core's token-style speed limiter (already token-style per the project description) for System.Threading.RateLimiting's TokenBucketRateLimiter to get a tested, first-party implementation with proper AutoReplenishment instead of maintaining custom bucket math — likely a small, low-risk refactor issue

Evaluate System.IO.Pipelines for the socket-to-disk hot path per download segment if profiling shows GC pressure from repeated buffer allocation in the current HttpClient-stream-to-FileStream copy loop; note this is a bigger architectural change than the RandomAccess/RateLimiter swaps and should be scoped as its own performance-investigation issue with before/after allocation benchmarks

name: Internet Download Manager (IDM)
popularity: One of the most widely used commercial download accelerators since the early 2000s; still actively sold/updated (v6.4x as of 2026). No public source/star count since closed source.
architecture: Native Windows app with a background download engine plus a small native browser-integration bridge process ("IDM Integration Module") that talks to browser extensions (Chrome/Firefox/Edge/Opera/Safari) via a native-messaging-like bridge and hands off intercepted download URLs to the engine. Segments are not fixed at start; the engine maintains a live map of segment ranges per file and dynamically rebalances them as connections become free. It periodically flushes segment boundaries/offsets to a resume/state file (multiple times per minute) so pause, crash, or power loss can resume without re-verifying the whole file. Scheduling is a separate subsystem that can trigger connect/disconnect, queue start/stop, and shutdown at specific times, independent of the segment engine. A separate 'media grabber' component hooks into browser page network activity heuristically to detect streaming media URLs.
standout_features: Dynamic mid-flight segmentation: instead of pre-splitting a file into N fixed ranges before download starts, IDM always finds the current largest unfinished segment and bisects it whenever a new connection slot frees up — this keeps every connection busy until the very end and avoids the classic 'one thread starves while others finish' tail-latency problem of static range-splitting.
Frequent (sub-minute) persistence of segment progress so resume after crash/power-loss is exact, not just at pause time.

Native browser-integration bridge + extension architecture that intercepts downloads at the browser network-request layer and hands them to the desktop engine, rather than relying on the browser's own download UI.
Independent scheduler subsystem (time-based connect/download/disconnect/shutdown) decoupled from the transfer engine.
Visual segment map (color-coded: boundary/downloaded/pending) exposed to the user for transparency into engine behavior.
ideas_for_kurio: Replace Kurio.Core's (likely static) up-front N-way range split with a dynamic 'largest remaining segment bisection' rebalancer: track segment state as a list of (start,end,downloaded) ranges per download; whenever a worker task completes its range early or a new connection slot opens (e.g., speed-limit token frees up, or a stalled connection is retried), pick the segment with the largest remaining byte count and split it in half, assigning the new half to the new/free connection.

Change the JSON resume/state schema to persist the full live segment map (not just overall bytes-downloaded) with a periodic flush interval (e.g., every 5-10s or every N MB) via a background timer, so SIGKILL/crash mid-download resumes at exact per-segment offsets instead of re-downloading whole chunks.

Add a SignalR event (e.g., SegmentMapChanged) that streams the current segment map to Kurio.Web so the dashboard can render a live per-file progress bar broken into colored segments, mirroring IDM's transparency UX.

Add an independent scheduling module (new Kurio.Core.Scheduling or a hosted service) supporting cron-like or one-shot time windows to start/pause a queue, decoupled from the download engine itself — expose via REST endpoints and a Blazor scheduler page.

Design a browser-capture story as a small native-messaging host (a lightweight .NET console app) + a browser extension that POSTs intercepted URLs to Kurio.Server's REST API, rather than trying to build this into the server itself.
pitfalls_to_avoid: Don't tie segment rebalancing decisions to wall-clock timers alone — trigger rebalancing on connection-completion events to avoid idle workers waiting for the next poll tick.
Persisting segment state too infrequently risks large re-download on crash; too frequently risks I/O contention — make the flush interval configurable and byte-threshold-based, not just time-based.

name: Free Download Manager (FDM)
repo: https://www.freedownloadmanager.org/ (closed-source current v6.x binary; older 3.x/5.x lineage had open-source roots, no longer actively public on GitHub)
popularity: Long-running (20+ years), widely distributed cross-platform (Windows/macOS/Linux/Android) freeware; large install base via download portals, but not a transparent open-source project today — no public star count.
architecture: Desktop app with an integrated BitTorrent client, HTTP/FTP downloader, and built-in media previewer, plus a browser extension ('Download with FDM') for Chrome/Firefox that intercepts links similarly to IDM's model. Traffic shaping is implemented as selectable global bandwidth-usage modes (e.g., unlimited / limited / scheduled-limited) applied engine-wide rather than per-download. A smart scheduler triggers start/pause of downloads, launching arbitrary applications, and connect/disconnect of the network interface at specific times.
standout_features: Multiple selectable 'traffic usage modes' that let a user quickly switch between full-speed, bandwidth-capped, and time-windowed throttling profiles instead of manually setting a numeric limit each time.
Built-in BitTorrent + HTTP(S) + media-grab support unified under one queue/UI.
Smart scheduler that can also launch external applications and toggle the network connection, not just start/stop downloads.
Browser add-on ecosystem for site-specific video/file capture.
ideas_for_kurio: Instead of Kurio's speed-limiter exposing only a raw bytes/sec numeric field, add named 'bandwidth profiles' (Unlimited, Throttled-Background, Scheduled-Quiet-Hours) that map to token-bucket configs, selectable from the dashboard and switchable without editing raw numbers.
Extend scheduling ideas (shared with IDM) to include a post-download action hook (e.g., run a script/webhook, shut down the orchestration host) — useful for headless server deployments of Kurio.

Consider a queue-level (not just global) traffic-shaping mode so different queues (e.g., 'bulk ISO downloads' vs 'interactive user downloads') can have independent shaping profiles feeding into the same token-bucket limiter engine.
pitfalls_to_avoid: Avoid conflating bandwidth mode switching with restarting active transfers — profile changes should hot-apply to the existing token bucket, not require pausing/resuming downloads.

FDM's plugin/add-on story is thin on public documentation; don't assume there's a stable extension API to emulate — treat 'plugin system' as an open design problem for Kurio rather than copying a concrete FDM mechanism.

name: GNU Wget2
repo: gnuwget/wget2 (mirrored at rockdaboot/wget2; canonical dev on GitLab gnuwget/wget2)
popularity: Official GNU successor to wget1; actively maintained (releases through 2024+, e.g., 2.2.0), moderate GitHub presence (a few hundred stars across mirrors) but authoritative as the GNU project.
architecture: Complete rewrite split into libwget (LGPLv3+, reusable core client library) and the wget2 CLI (GPLv3+) that wraps it — a clean library/CLI separation Kurio should note even though Kurio already has this via Kurio.Core. Multithreaded by design: parallel download threads plus intra-file multithreaded chunked download via --chunk-size, unlike wget1's single-threaded, single-connection-per-file model. Networking layer supports HTTP/2 multiplexing (via nghttp2 + GnuTLS ALPN, including streaming/pipelining), TCP Fast Open for both plaintext and TLS, TLS session resumption with a persistent session cache, and transparent decompression (gzip, deflate, bzip2, xz/lzma, brotli, zstandard). It supports Metalink (RFC 5854/6249, Metalink3) for mirror selection and checksum verification, letting it fetch a file from multiple mirrors and verify integrity automatically.
standout_features: Clean library (libwget) vs CLI separation with permissive LGPL core so the engine can be embedded elsewhere.
--chunk-size: intra-file multithreaded chunked downloads as a first-class CLI flag, not just multi-file parallelism.
HTTP/2 multiplexing used to reduce connection count while still parallelizing streams.
TCP Fast Open on both HTTP and HTTPS to cut a round-trip on new connections.
Persistent TLS session-resumption cache surviving across process runs.
Native Metalink support for automatic multi-mirror + checksum-verified downloads.
Broad transparent decompression support (including modern brotli/zstd) applied automatically based on server response headers.
ideas_for_kurio: Add HTTP/2 awareness to Kurio.Core's segmented downloader: when the origin server negotiates HTTP/2 (or HTTP/3) via SocketsHttpHandler, prefer fewer TCP connections and rely on stream multiplexing for parallel range requests instead of opening N raw sockets — SocketsHttpHandler.EnableMultipleHttp2Connections and per-request PooledConnectionLifetime tuning are the relevant knobs.

Persist and reuse a TLS session cache across app restarts (SslClientAuthenticationOptions / QUIC session ticket reuse where supported) to shave handshake latency on resumed downloads to the same host, mirroring wget2's persistent session-resumption cache.

Add a Metalink-like 'multi-mirror' download mode to Kurio.Core: accept multiple candidate URLs for the same logical file, race/split segments across mirrors, and use the existing checksum-verification feature to validate the assembled result regardless of which mirror served which byte range.

Ensure Kurio.Core transparently handles Content-Encoding (gzip/deflate/br) via HttpClient's decompression handler, and consider adding zstd support (System.IO.Compression added Brotli/ZLib but not Zstd natively — would need a library) for large asset downloads.
Expose a --chunk-size-equivalent server-side setting (segment size threshold) so operators can tune how aggressively small files get split vs. downloaded as a single connection.
pitfalls_to_avoid: Don't assume more TCP connections always equals more throughput once HTTP/2 is in play — multiplexed streams over one connection can outperform many raw sockets and reduce origin server load/rate-limit hits.

wget2's chunk-size multithreading works because it treats each chunk as an independent GET with Range headers reassembled at the end — Kurio's engine should ensure Range-request support is verified (Accept-Ranges header + 206 Partial Content) before attempting segmentation, falling back to single-stream download otherwise, same as wget2/IDM/curl all do.

name: curl / libcurl
popularity: Extremely widely deployed (billions of installations, virtually every OS/embedded device); very actively maintained by Daniel Stenberg and a large contributor base; one of the most battle-tested C networking codebases in existence.
architecture: libcurl exposes an Easy API (single blocking-style transfer, handle-based) and a Multi API (event-driven, manages many easy handles concurrently, non-blocking). Connection management is handled by an internal connection cache/pool per multi handle: on a new transfer, libcurl checks the pool for a reusable connection matched primarily by hostname plus port/protocol/other compatibility properties (proxy, TLS config, etc.) before opening a new socket. Idle connections are retained up to CURLOPT_MAXAGE_CONN (default 118s) and CURLOPT_MAXLIFETIME_CONN, with CURLMOPT_MAXCONNECTS bounding pool size (LRU eviction of oldest idle connection when full). Happy Eyeballs (RFC 8305) races IPv6/IPv4 connection attempts with a configurable head start (default 200ms via CURLOPT_HAPPY_EYEBALLS_TIMEOUT_MS) and uses whichever completes first, canceling the other. The CLI's -Z/--parallel mode drives many transfers through the multi interface at once (default cap 50 concurrent, tunable via --parallel-max, with a separate --parallel-max-host origin cap), preferring to multiplex/reuse existing connections over opening new ones unless --parallel-immediate is given. -C/--continue-at resumes a transfer from a specific byte offset (or auto-detects local file size with -C -), relying on server support for Range/Content-Range.
standout_features: Two-tier API (Easy/Multi) cleanly separating single-transfer semantics from a scalable concurrent-transfer event loop — directly analogous to a HttpClient-per-segment vs. an orchestrator pattern.
Connection pool keyed by hostname+port+protocol+config compatibility, with explicit idle-age and lifetime eviction knobs exposed to the caller.
Multi-API connection sharing across independently created/destroyed easy handles — connections outlive the handle that created them.
Happy Eyeballs dual-stack racing with a tunable head-start window, always preferring the first successful connection and killing the loser.

Parallel CLI mode with both a global concurrency cap and a per-origin concurrency cap, plus an explicit flag to opt out of connection-reuse-preferring behavior when raw throughput matters more than connection economy.
Simple, well-understood resume contract: --continue-at N sends Range: bytes=N- and trusts server Content-Range/206 response, with '-C -' auto-detecting the offset from an existing partial local file.
ideas_for_kurio: Model Kurio.Core's per-download connection strategy explicitly on curl's pool semantics: use a shared SocketsHttpHandler (or PooledConnectionLifetime-tuned HttpMessageInvoker) per origin host across all segments/downloads to that host, rather than a fresh HttpClient per segment — this gets connection reuse 'for free' but Kurio should add its own explicit per-host concurrency cap analogous to --parallel-max-host to avoid hammering a single origin across multiple simultaneous downloads in the queue.

Add a global + per-host concurrency cap to Kurio's queue engine (e.g., MaxConcurrentSegmentsGlobal and MaxConcurrentSegmentsPerHost config), mirroring --parallel-max / --parallel-max-host, configurable via the REST API/dashboard.

Adopt curl's resume contract as Kurio's canonical resume semantics: always resume via Range: bytes=<offset>- against the same URL, validate the server's 206 response and Content-Range/ETag/Last-Modified against the persisted state before trusting the local partial file, and fall back to a full restart if the server doesn't support ranges or the file changed (ETag mismatch) — this closes a real correctness gap many home-grown resume implementations get wrong.

Implement a Happy-Eyeballs-style connect race for dual-stack hosts if SocketsHttpHandler's built-in behavior isn't sufficient, or explicitly configure/verify .NET's own Happy Eyeballs support (available via SocketsHttpHandler/Socket connect since .NET has had some dual-stack support) rather than assuming it 'just works'.

Expose connection-pool tuning (idle timeout, max lifetime, max connections per host) as first-class Kurio.Core.Config options, since Polly-based retry sits on top of the transport and benefits from knowing these bounds when deciding retry vs. reconnect strategy.
pitfalls_to_avoid: Don't let Polly-driven retries and the HTTP connection pool fight each other — a naive retry-with-new-HttpClient pattern defeats connection reuse and re-triggers TLS handshakes; retries should reuse the same pooled handler/host.

Range-based resume must validate that the remote resource hasn't changed since the partial download started (ETag/Last-Modified check) before appending to a local partial file — silently trusting stale offsets can corrupt the reassembled file.

Per-origin concurrency caps must be considered across the whole queue, not just within a single multi-segment download — two simultaneous queued downloads from the same host each opening 8 segments can accidentally open 16 connections to one origin and get rate-limited/blocked.

name: aria2 (.aria2 control file / resume format)
popularity: ~25k+ GitHub stars, mature/stable, low-activity maintenance mode but widely deployed
architecture: Single-process CLI/daemon with optional JSON-RPC/XML-RPC server for remote control (session save/load, tellStatus, pause/unpause). Each active download gets a sidecar '<filename>.aria2' binary control file alongside the real (truncated-to-size or sparse) output file. The control file is the authoritative resume/progress record; the data file itself holds only the bytes actually written.
standout_features: Binary control file (not JSON/XML) versioned via a 2-bit VERSION field for forward/backward compatibility; v1 uses network byte order (big-endian) for all multi-byte ints, v0 used host byte order and is only read, never written, by modern aria2

Fields in order: VERSION, EXTENSION bitmask, INFO HASH LENGTH + INFO HASH (BitTorrent identity), PIECE LENGTH, TOTAL LENGTH, UPLOAD LENGTH, BITFIELD LENGTH + BITFIELD (one bit per whole piece, completed=1), NUMBER OF IN-FLIGHT PIECES, then for each in-flight piece: INDEX, LENGTH, PIECE BITFIELD LENGTH + PIECE BITFIELD (sub-piece granularity, 16KiB chunks) — this lets aria2 resume a piece that was only partially received rather than re-downloading the whole piece

Control file is flushed periodically during the transfer (on a save-interval timer) and always on graceful shutdown/pause; on restart aria2 reopens it, reconstructs the bitfield, and reissues HTTP Range requests only for missing byte ranges, using HTTP validators (If-Range/ETag) to detect a changed remote resource before trusting the local bitfield

--file-allocation flag exposes explicit tradeoffs: 'none' (sparse, fastest, fragmentation risk), 'prealloc' (posix_fallocate/fallocate, zero-fills, safe but slower to start on some FS), 'trunc' (ftruncate to final size, may create sparse holes), and 'falloc' (Linux fallocate(2), fast and safe where supported)

Known pitfall documented in aria2 issue #583: SetFileValidData on Windows was considered for fast preallocation but rejected because it can expose previously-deleted disk data (a security/privacy leak) unlike posix_fallocate/fallocate which always zero-fill
ideas_for_kurio: Adopt a compact, versioned binary (or MessagePack) per-download sidecar '<file>.kurio-state' with an explicit VERSION byte so the schema can evolve without breaking old resumes; keep a human-debuggable JSON fallback only for the queue/job list, not per-segment state

Store segment completion as a bitfield over fixed-size sub-ranges (e.g. 256KB-1MB chunks) rather than only 'bytesDownloaded per segment', so a segment that died mid-flight can resume from its last fully-written chunk instead of restarting the whole segment

On resume, before trusting the local bitfield/segment map, issue a HEAD (or small ranged GET) and compare ETag/Last-Modified/Content-Length against values captured at download start; if mismatched, invalidate the whole state file and restart (mirrors aria2 + wget2 behavior)
Flush the state file on a timer (e.g. every 1-2s) AND on every pause/cancel/shutdown, decoupled from the data-file fsync cadence, so state-file writes stay cheap even though full data fsync is rarer

Never use SetFileValidData equivalents for prealloc on Windows; use FileStream/RandomAccess preallocationSize (which maps to SetFileInformationByHandle FILE_ALLOCATION_INFO, zero-semantics preserved) or expose an explicit opt-in 'fast prealloc' flag with a security warning if you ever add a raw SetFileValidData path
pitfalls_to_avoid: Do not roll your own binary format without a version field — aria2's v0->v1 byte-order change shows why versioning from day one matters
Do not treat 'file exists with expected size' as proof of a valid resume — always re-validate ETag/Last-Modified before reusing partial data
Avoid fast Windows preallocation APIs that skip zero-fill unless you fully understand the data-leak implications

name: wget2 (partial-download resume via .wget-hsts-independent sidecar / HTTP validators)
popularity: Official GNU successor to wget; actively maintained, moderate community size (not primarily a GitHub star-count project)
architecture: Single-shot CLI process (no daemon/RPC); resume state for a partial file is largely stateless with respect to sidecar metadata — wget2 relies on the local file's size (bytes already on disk) plus HTTP conditional-request headers, not a separate structured state file, to decide how to continue a '-c/--continue' download.
standout_features: Uses If-Range combined with either ETag or Last-Modified (per RFC 7233, never both) to make the Range request conditional: server returns 206 to continue, or 200 (full body) if the resource changed, which wget2 detects and restarts the file from scratch

--continue simply appends from Content-Length-so-far; there is an open wget2 issue/dev-thread (#580/703) about wget2 not tracking sufficient metadata (like true completion state vs. truncated/corrupt file) which causes ambiguity — a caution about being too minimal
No piece-level or segment-level resume tracking at all (wget2 is single-stream per file by default) — this is the naive baseline Kurio already exceeds with segmented downloads
ideas_for_kurio: Persist the validator (ETag and/or Last-Modified) captured on the initial 200/206 response as part of the per-download state file; use If-Range on every resumed range request so the server itself can reject a stale resume with a fresh 200, which Kurio should detect (Content-Length/Range headers absent) and treat as 'must restart'

Add an explicit 'download integrity' field distinguishing 'segment fully written' vs 'segment file size matches expected but never fsynced/verified' to avoid wget2-style ambiguity about truncated/corrupt continuations
Log and surface to the SignalR dashboard when a resume falls back to full restart because the remote resource changed, rather than silently starting over
pitfalls_to_avoid: Relying only on file size on disk as proof of correct partial content (no checksum/validator) risks silently resuming corrupted or stale data, exactly the ambiguity wget2 contributors flagged

name: Free Download Manager (.fdmdownload sidecar file)
popularity: Long-running proprietary/closed-core product (20+ years), large end-user base, Windows/macOS/Android/browser-extension ecosystem
language: C++ (closed source; behavior inferred from file-extension docs and community reports)
architecture: Desktop GUI app; while a file is downloading (including multi-connection segmented downloads), FDM writes to a single '<filename>.fdmdownload' file that embeds both the partial content and enough metadata for FDM to know the file is incomplete; the extension itself acts as the 'incomplete' marker so other tools/OS file managers can visually flag unfinished downloads, and FDM swaps it for the real filename only on verified completion.
standout_features: Single-file design: rather than separate '<file>.part' + '<file>.state.json', the sidecar convention embeds an unambiguous incomplete/complete signal directly in the filesystem namespace (extension), simplifying crash recovery — after a crash, any '*.fdmdownload' file left in the download directory is self-evidently resumable/incomplete

Supports resuming multi-connection (segmented) downloads from the same sidecar, implying internal per-segment offset bookkeeping even though the on-disk artifact is a single growing file rather than multiple temp files
FDM explicitly renames to the final name only after the transfer is confirmed complete — a simple, robust 'commit' step that avoids ever exposing a half-written file under its final name
ideas_for_kurio: Adopt the same 'incomplete marker' convention for the final artifact: write to '<file>.kurio-part' (or keep the state file's existence as the marker) and only rename/move to the final filename after all segments are verified (checksum, if available) and fsynced — this gives Kurio a crash-safe, filesystem-visible 'this download is still in progress' signal

Ensure the rename-to-final step is atomic (File.Move with overwrite on the same volume) and happens strictly after the state file is marked 'Completed' and (optionally) deleted, so a crash between data-flush and rename can't leave an inconsistent final file
pitfalls_to_avoid: Don't rename to the final filename before checksum verification and full fsync complete — otherwise a crash mid-rename or a premature 'done' UI signal can hand the user a corrupt file that looks finished

name: .NET RandomAccess / File.OpenHandle parallel positional I/O (BCL feature, .NET 6+)
popularity: Core BCL feature since .NET 6; actively maintained, used across the .NET ecosystem
architecture: Provides stateless, offset-based file I/O (System.IO.RandomAccess) built on a shared SafeFileHandle so multiple threads/tasks can read/write at independent offsets concurrently without the position-mutation races FileStream has; File.OpenHandle exposes a preallocationSize parameter that maps to platform-native preallocation (posix_fallocate/fallocate on Linux, fcntl F_PREALLOCATE-family on macOS, SetFileInformationByHandle FILE_ALLOCATION_INFO on Windows) and supports scatter/gather I/O (writing/reading many buffers in one syscall).
standout_features: RandomAccess.Write/WriteAsync(SafeFileHandle, buffer, fileOffset) — thread-safe positional writes with no shared file-pointer state, ideal for N parallel segment downloaders writing into disjoint byte ranges of one shared handle

File.OpenHandle(..., preallocationSize: totalSize) preallocates the whole file up front using zero-filling native APIs (safe semantics, unlike SetFileValidData) reducing fragmentation and avoiding late 'disk full' failures mid-download
Scatter/gather overloads (ReadOnlyMemory<byte>[] buffers in a single WriteAsync call) reduce syscall count when flushing several small buffered chunks belonging to one segment together

RandomAccess.FlushToDisk(handle) / FileStream.Flush(flushToDisk:true) give explicit control to decouple 'data is written to OS cache' from 'data is durable on disk' — letting an app choose a cheap progress-checkpoint cadence (write + update in-memory/state-file progress) independent of an expensive fsync cadence (e.g., fsync only every N MB or every checkpoint interval, not per chunk)
ideas_for_kurio: Replace any per-segment FileStream instances with a single shared SafeFileHandle per download (opened once via File.OpenHandle with preallocationSize = total content length when known) and have each segment worker call RandomAccess.WriteAsync at its own offset — eliminates the need for per-segment temp files and a final merge/copy pass entirely

Decouple checkpoint cadence from fsync cadence explicitly in the writer pipeline: update the in-memory progress/bitfield and persist the lightweight state-file JSON frequently (e.g. every 250ms-1s or every N bytes), but only call RandomAccess.FlushToDisk on a coarser interval (e.g. every 5-10s or every completed segment) to avoid fsync thrashing on spinning disks/NAS/SMB shares

When total content length is unknown (no Content-Length / chunked response), fall back to no-preallocation (sparse growth) or an estimated preallocation with post-hoc truncate, and record in the state file which mode was used so resume logic knows whether to trust file length as a completion signal

Add a configurable IStorageAllocationStrategy (None/Sparse/Preallocate) in Kurio.Core so behavior can be tuned per filesystem (e.g., avoid preallocation on SMB/NAS mounts where it forces a full-size synchronous transfer per the APFS/SMB sparse-file caveat, and where fallocate over network filesystems can be slow or unsupported)

Explicitly avoid any P/Invoke to SetFileValidData for 'fast' Windows preallocation; standardize on File.OpenHandle's built-in preallocationSize which already selects the safe, zero-filling FILE_ALLOCATION_INFO path
pitfalls_to_avoid: Per-segment temp files merged at the end double the disk I/O (write once per segment, then read+write again to merge) and roughly double peak disk usage during the merge — prefer shared-handle positional writes over this pattern for Kurio.Core

Memory-mapped files are a poor fit for this workload: they complicate flush/checkpoint semantics (dirty-page flush timing is OS-controlled and less predictable than explicit fsync calls) and don't offer material benefit over RandomAccess for large sequential-ish segment writes

fsync'ing after every write call will tank throughput on rotational disks and especially on SMB/NAS mounts; but never fsync until 'download complete' risks large data loss windows on crash — pick a bounded time/byte-based fsync interval and make it configurable

On APFS, F_PREALLOCATE can fail with EINVAL in some configurations, and sparse files lose their sparseness when copied over SMB — don't assume preallocation always succeeds; treat it as best-effort and fall back gracefully

name: aria2
popularity: ~25k GitHub stars; C++ project, mature but low-activity (mostly maintenance mode as of 2026, sporadic commits, many stale PRs)
architecture: Single-process, event-loop based (libuv/epoll) multi-protocol downloader (HTTP/HTTPS/FTP/SFTP/BitTorrent/Metalink) exposing a JSON-RPC/XML-RPC/WebSocket control API (aria2.addUri, aria2.tellStatus, aria2.pause, aria2.changeOption, aria2.getGlobalStat, system.multicall, etc.) so any GUI/CLI can drive it as a headless daemon — architecturally the closest analog to a 'Kurio.Core engine + separate UI' split. Per-download state and per-segment progress are persisted in a sidecar '<file>.aria2' control file (binary format storing piece bitfield, URIs, and in-flight segment offsets) so downloads survive process restart even without a full session file. `--save-session` additionally serializes the whole queue (GIDs, URIs, options) to a text file consumable via `--input-file` for restoring an entire batch. Segment/connection strategy is decoupled from source count via `--split` (target total connections) and `--min-split-size` (floor before further splitting is refused), with a pluggable `--uri-selector` (inorder/feedback/adaptive) that does mirror failover and can persist observed per-server throughput stats (`--server-stat-of/-if`) to bias future mirror choice.
standout_features: Control-file-per-download (.aria2) storing segment bitfield/offsets so resume works even after a hard crash with no full session file
Adaptive URI selector (inorder/feedback/adaptive) that tracks per-server historical throughput across runs to pick mirrors, not just round-robin
--always-resume / --max-resume-failure-tries: explicit policy for what to do when some mirrors advertise no-resume support and others do

Full Metalink4 (RFC 5854, .meta4/.metalink XML) support: mirror lists, per-piece hashes for chunk-level integrity checking, language/os/location file-variant selection, and realtime chunk checksum validation during transfer, independent from Metalink/HTTP header variant (RFC 6249)
RPC-first design: the daemon is fully controllable/observable over JSON-RPC, decoupling engine from any particular UI — same shape as Kurio.Server's SignalR hubs
ideas_for_kurio: Add a per-download sidecar '.kurio' or '.progress.json' control file (segment bitfield + byte offsets) written incrementally during transfer, separate from the full queue-state JSON, so a crash mid-segment doesn't require re-probing the whole file — only the in-flight segment is re-verified

Implement an aria2-style resume policy option: when Accept-Ranges/206 support differs across configured mirrors for one download, decide (config-driven) whether to fall back to single-connection full re-download vs. abort vs. skip that mirror

Add a pluggable mirror/URI selector strategy on DownloadTask (in-order, fastest-observed, adaptive) and persist rolling per-host throughput stats so future downloads to the same host pick better initial segment counts

Implement RFC 5854 Metalink (.meta4) parsing as an optional import path: user pastes/uploads a .meta4 file, Kurio.Core extracts mirrors + per-piece hashes and drives the existing segmented engine with multi-source failover instead of single-URL segments

Expose a minimal JSON-RPC-style bulk/scripting API (mirroring aria2.* method shapes) alongside the existing REST+SignalR API for headless/automation clients, since this is a well-trodden interface shape worth being compatible-ish with
pitfalls_to_avoid: Don't couple the segment count strictly to number of mirrors — aria2 decouples '--split' (connections) from the URI list and reuses URIs round-robin, which Kurio.Core's engine should already support conceptually
Avoid a monolithic single full-session file for everything; a crash while writing it can corrupt in-flight-segment info for all downloads, not just one

name: wget2
popularity: ~1.4k GitHub stars, actively maintained successor to GNU Wget (development happens primarily on GitLab, mirrored to GitHub)
architecture: Uses libwget as the core HTTP/FTP engine with libnghttp2 for HTTP/2 (ALPN-negotiated) including request pipelining/multiplexing, and can multithread a single large file download by splitting it into fixed-size chunks (`--chunk-size`) each fetched by a worker thread issuing its own Range request, rather than a fixed connection count — chunk size, not connection count, is the tunable. Supports Metalink both as XML description (RFC 5854, versions 3 and 4) and as the HTTP-header variant (RFC 6249: Link rel=duplicate + Digest instance headers), letting it discover mirrors/hashes without fetching a separate .meta4 file.
standout_features: --chunk-size based splitting (fixed chunk size rather than fixed connection count) so segment count scales with file size automatically

First-class HTTP/2 multiplexing via nghttp2 for regular fetches, plus TCP Fast Open, TLS session resumption cache, and TLS False Start for reducing per-connection setup latency — directly relevant to whether Kurio should open N sockets or N HTTP/2 streams per segment
Implements RFC 6249 Metalink/HTTP (mirrors/hashes discovered via response headers on the primary URL, no separate metadata file needed) in addition to RFC 5854 XML metalink
ideas_for_kurio: When probing a URL, in addition to checking Accept-Ranges/Content-Length, inspect response for Link: <mirror-url>; rel=duplicate and Digest: SHA-256=... headers (RFC 6249) and opportunistically add discovered mirrors as failover sources for the same segmented download, without requiring the user to supply a .meta4 file

Make Kurio.Core's segmentation strategy chunk-size-driven (e.g. target ~8-16MB per segment, split count = ceil(size/chunkSize) capped by max-connections) instead of a purely fixed segment count, so small files don't over-fragment and huge files scale connections sensibly

For HTTP/2 origins, evaluate using multiple concurrent GET-with-Range requests over the *same* multiplexed connection (via HttpClient with EnableMultipleHttp2Connections=false) instead of opening N TCP connections, since RFC 9113 recommends one connection per origin for HTTP/2 — document this as an explicit design decision in Kurio.Core's connection strategy
pitfalls_to_avoid: Don't assume HTTP/2 multiplexed streams behave like independent HTTP/1.1 sockets for throughput purposes — a single slow/misbehaving stream or a low SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS can throttle all 'segments' sharing one HTTP/2 connection differently than parallel HTTP/1.1 sockets would

name: Motrix (Turbo v2, in beta)
popularity: ~40k+ GitHub stars for classic Motrix v1 (Electron+aria2 wrapper); v2 'Motrix Turbo' is an active from-scratch rewrite in beta as of 2026
language: TypeScript (Electron/React UI) + Node.js core, historically wrapping a forked aria2 C++ binary
architecture: Layered design explicitly separating a portable download core from the UI: the core exposes MDXP (Motrix Download eXchange Protocol), an open JSON-RPC 2.0 wire protocol with Zod-validated schemas, so the same core process can be driven by the Electron desktop UI, a headless Node/Docker server with its own web UI, an official CLI (`@motrix/cli`), or browser extensions (Manifest V3 native messaging) — architecturally very close to Kurio.Server (engine) + Kurio.Web (Blazor) + potential future headless/CLI clients. Session/download state is persisted in SQLite (better-sqlite3) rather than flat JSON files, enabling queryable history and automatic restore of in-flight downloads after a restart. A QuickJS-sandboxed plugin system (with a manifest schema, permission model, and an in-app marketplace) allows third parties to add filename templates, page-scraping link extraction, and site-specific media resolvers without touching core code.
standout_features: MDXP: a documented, versioned JSON-RPC 2.0 protocol (with a standalone npm package of shared Zod types) as the single integration surface for desktop UI, CLI, browser extension, and remote/headless pairing — not just an internal implementation detail
SQLite-backed session storage instead of a JSON blob, giving atomic writes, queryability, and safer partial-update semantics under crash/restart
Device-code pairing flow for CLI/agent clients to authenticate against a remote/headless instance — a lightweight secure-pairing pattern for exposing a control API beyond localhost
QuickJS sandboxed plugin architecture with a formal manifest + permission schema and a public plugin registry JSON feed

Browser extension hand-off (Manifest V3 native messaging) that intercepts browser downloads and redirects them to the engine — this is exactly the 'browser integration / clipboard capture' backlog item Kurio has open
ideas_for_kurio: Define an explicit, versioned wire-protocol contract (analogous to MDXP) for Kurio's SignalR hub payloads and REST DTOs — publish it as a small shared contracts package/NuGet so future CLI or browser-extension clients aren't reverse-engineering hub method shapes

Replace or supplement Kurio.Core's JSON state-persistence file with SQLite (e.g. via Microsoft.Data.Sqlite or EF Core) for the download queue/history, giving atomic per-row updates and safe concurrent access from multiple server components instead of full-file JSON rewrites on every progress tick

Design the future browser-integration backlog item around a native-messaging-style handoff: a small browser extension posts intercepted download URLs (with cookies/auth headers) to Kurio.Server's REST API, mirroring Motrix's Manifest V3 native messaging approach

For a future plugin/extension system backlog item, look at Motrix's manifest+permission-schema+sandbox approach (even if .NET would use AssemblyLoadContext or a WASM sandbox instead of QuickJS) as a reference shape: declarative manifest, explicit permission grants, marketplace-style discovery feed
pitfalls_to_avoid: Motrix v1's tight coupling to a bundled/forked aria2 binary became a maintenance burden significant enough to justify a full v2 rewrite — avoid baking Kurio.Core's segmented-download logic around a similarly hard external dependency; keep it a pure managed-code engine as it already is

The v2 rewrite is still in beta with explicit 'do not use with your only copy of v1 data' warnings — a lesson that persistence-format migrations (JSON to SQLite, etc.) need an explicit, tested migration/backup path before shipping

name: Internet Download Manager (IDM) — dynamic segmentation algorithm
popularity: Proprietary, decades-old commercial product; extremely widely used on Windows; not open source but its segmentation algorithm is publicly documented
language: C/C++ (closed source; behavior documented by vendor)
architecture: Not applicable in the open-source sense — included purely as a documented reference algorithm for adaptive/dynamic segmentation rather than a codebase to study directly.
standout_features: Dynamic segmentation: instead of pre-splitting a file into N fixed segments before starting, IDM starts a connection, and each time a *new* connection becomes available it finds the currently-largest remaining segment and splits it in half, assigning the new half to the new connection

Idle-connection work stealing: when a connection finishes its segment early and the next connection hasn't started its own segment yet, IDM reassigns/merges that segment back onto the free connection instead of leaving it idle
Split-refusal floor: IDM will not split a segment further once it is 'too small for this connection type', preventing pathological over-fragmentation on fast/low-latency links
ideas_for_kurio: Implement IDM-style dynamic re-segmentation in Kurio.Core: when a segment worker finishes early and no unstarted segment is queued, split the largest remaining in-progress segment's unread tail in half and hand the new half to the freed worker (requires making segment boundaries mid-flight-adjustable rather than fixed at download start)
Add a minimum-remaining-bytes floor (e.g. skip further splitting below ~1-2MB remaining) to Kurio's segment planner to avoid thrashing on fast connections where per-request overhead would dominate
Expose 'segments rebalanced N times' as a stat in Kurio.Core's stats/ETA module so users/operators can see the adaptive algorithm working, distinct from static per-segment throughput
pitfalls_to_avoid: A fixed segment count decided once at download start (Kurio's current apparent model) leaves fast workers idle near the end while a slow worker's segment is still large — this is precisely the inefficiency IDM's algorithm targets; worth an explicit backlog issue even if not implemented immediately

name: .NET SocketsHttpHandler / HttpClient HTTP/2+HTTP/3 range behavior
popularity: Built-in BCL component, actively developed (net10.0 docs current as of 2026)
architecture: SocketsHttpHandler pools connections per-origin; for HTTP/1.1 it opens multiple TCP connections up to MaxConnectionsPerServer, making 'one connection per segment' natural. For HTTP/2, RFC 9113 says clients SHOULD use a single connection per origin, and .NET honors that by default (only one HTTP/2 connection to a given server) with concurrent requests multiplexed as separate streams on it — EnableMultipleHttp2Connections must be explicitly set true to open extra HTTP/2 connections, and even then each connection is still capped by the server's SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS. PooledConnectionLifetime/PooledConnectionIdleTimeout control connection recycling, which matters for long-running segmented downloads against CDNs that rotate edge nodes or invalidate signed URLs.
standout_features: EnableMultipleHttp2Connections: an explicit, documented opt-in to violate the 'one connection per origin' HTTP/2 norm — directly answers the 'connection-per-segment vs multiplexing' design question for Kurio.Core

Per-origin connection pooling with PooledConnectionLifetime, useful for forcing periodic reconnects on very long segmented downloads (helps pick up DNS/CDN changes and avoid a single connection silently degrading)

HttpRequestMessage.Version + VersionPolicy (RequestVersionOrLower/Exact/OrHigher) let Kurio.Core explicitly force HTTP/1.1 per-segment sockets even against an HTTP/2-capable server if that's empirically faster for large parallel range downloads
ideas_for_kurio: In Kurio.Core's segment-worker connection setup, detect the negotiated protocol version of the first probe/HEAD request; if HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, either set EnableMultipleHttp2Connections=true deliberately (with a comment referencing RFC 9113) or fall back to forcing HTTP/1.1 via VersionPolicy for the actual segment requests — don't let this be accidental/default behavior

Set PooledConnectionLifetime to a bounded value (e.g. a few minutes) on the HttpClient/SocketsHttpHandler instance used for segment workers so multi-hour downloads periodically re-resolve DNS and re-negotiate, catching CDN edge-node or signed-URL-expiry issues before they silently stall a segment

Add an explicit integration test that downloads a large file from an HTTP/2-only test server with 4+ concurrent Range requests and asserts they land on the expected number of streams/connections, to lock in whichever policy is chosen and catch accidental regressions when .NET's HTTP/2 defaults change across SDK versions
pitfalls_to_avoid: Silently relying on default SocketsHttpHandler behavior against an unknown-protocol server means segment 'connections' may actually be multiplexed HTTP/2 streams sharing one socket and one congestion-control state — segment-level throughput measurements and per-segment retry/backoff logic can be misleading unless this is explicitly accounted for
MaxConnectionsPerServer defaults and HTTP/2's single-connection norm interact poorly if Kurio.Core's segment planner assumes N segments == N independent network paths

name: Metalink standards family (RFC 5854 Metalink XML, RFC 6249 Metalink/HTTP)
popularity: IETF-standardized (2010/2011); adoption is now mostly limited to aria2 and wget2 among actively maintained clients — Apache Traffic Server ships a Metalink plugin server-side; most other download managers (FDM, IDM, browsers) do not implement it
architecture: RFC 5854 defines a .meta4 XML document format describing one logical file via a list of mirror <url> elements (each optionally with priority/location/geographic hints) plus per-file and optionally per-piece <hash> elements (multiple algorithms allowed, client should pick the strongest) and optional XML signatures for the metadata itself. RFC 6249 achieves the same mirror/hash discovery without a separate file by adding a `Digest:` response header (RFC 3230-style instance digest) and/or `Link: <url>; rel=duplicate` header(s) to the ordinary HTTP response for the resource itself, letting a client that only ever requested the resource directly still discover mirrors and validate integrity.
standout_features: Per-piece hashing in .meta4 enables detecting and re-downloading only the corrupted chunk of an already-completed file rather than re-verifying/re-fetching the whole thing
RFC 6249's Digest-header route requires no separate metadata fetch or file format at all — mirrors/hashes ride along on the normal response to the primary URL
Location/OS/language file-variant selection in .meta4 lets one metadata document describe several download variants (e.g. per-locale installers) and let the client auto-pick
ideas_for_kurio: Add an optional .meta4/.metalink importer to Kurio.Core: parse mirrors + per-piece hashes, feed them into the existing segmented-download engine as a multi-source job with per-segment hash verification instead of only a single end-to-end checksum

Add lightweight RFC 6249 header sniffing (Digest + Link rel=duplicate) to the existing probe/HEAD step so even plain single-URL downloads opportunistically pick up mirror/hash metadata with zero user effort, falling back silently when absent

When implementing per-piece hashes, size pieces independently from network segment size (a piece boundary doesn't have to equal a connection's byte-range boundary) so re-verification granularity can be tuned separately from parallelism
pitfalls_to_avoid: Low real-world adoption means test URLs are scarce — plan to stand up a local test server (e.g. a small ASP.NET Core endpoint) that emits RFC 6249 headers and serves a .meta4 fixture, rather than relying on finding public example URLs

RFC 6249 explicitly requires clients to treat Digest and Link rel=duplicate as independent, optionally-absent hints — don't require both to be present, and don't fail parsing on any unrecognized Link relation types

name: qBittorrent WebUI API
popularity: Very high (~28k+ stars), actively maintained; the de-facto lingua franca for *arr download-client integrations
language: C++ (server), API is JSON over HTTP
architecture: Single desktop/headless (qbittorrent-nox) process embeds an HTTP server exposing a versioned REST-ish API under /api/v2/<namespace>/<method> (namespaces: auth, app, log, sync, transfer, torrents, search, rss). Auth is cookie-based (POST /api/v2/auth/login sets a SID cookie); v5.2+ adds a Bearer API key that skips the cookie dance entirely. All mutating calls are POST, all reads are GET, and every method requires the prior auth except login. There's no separate client/server split - the WebUI and the RPC API are served by the same process.
standout_features: Version-namespaced flat method space (/api/v2/torrents/info, /api/v2/torrents/add, /api/v2/torrents/pause, /api/v2/torrents/setCategory) that is trivial to reverse-engineer and mock

Rich per-torrent state machine surfaced directly in JSON (state field: downloading/stalledDL/queuedDL/pausedDL/error/missingFiles/checkingUP/forcedUP/moving, etc.) which *arr apps poll to decide when an item is 'complete' and importable

Category and Tag as two independent, orthogonal classification axes, with categories carrying a savePath used for per-category output directories - this is exactly the mechanism *arr apps rely on to route completed downloads
content_path / save_path returned per-torrent so a caller (Sonarr/Radarr) can locate output files without guessing
File-level priority endpoint (filePrio) enabling selective download within one job

Because the API is so widely cloned (rdt-client emulates it fully just to appear as a 'normal' qBittorrent client to Sonarr/Radarr), implementing a qBittorrent-compatible shim is the single highest-leverage way for a new download server to plug into the existing *arr ecosystem without Sonarr/Radarr needing a new integration written
ideas_for_kurio: Ship an optional qBittorrent-API-compatibility controller in Kurio.Server (a distinct route prefix, e.g. /qbtcompat/api/v2/...) that maps Kurio's job model onto the qBittorrent v2 JSON shapes (torrents/info, add, pause, resume, delete, categories) purely so Sonarr/Radarr can add Kurio as a 'qBittorrent' download client with zero changes on their side - file this as its own GitHub issue since it's high-value and self-contained
Adopt qBittorrent's category=savePath convention for Kurio.Core's queue model so a future *arr integration (native or via the compat shim) can route by category to distinct output folders

Expose an equivalent to content_path/save_path plus a normalized status enum (downloading/paused/queued/completed/error) on every Kurio job returned via SignalR/REST, since that is the minimum vocabulary any *arr-style consumer will poll for

Support both cookie-session auth and a static Bearer API key on Kurio.Server, mirroring qBittorrent v5.2's simplification - the API key path is much friendlier for scripts, *arr apps, and Docker health checks
pitfalls_to_avoid: Don't invent a bespoke auth scheme for the primary API - offer a simple static API key first, since most self-hosted tooling (and the *arr ecosystem) expects that pattern
Keep the compat layer strictly additive/optional so it doesn't constrain Kurio's native REST/SignalR API design

name: SABnzbd API
popularity: High (~2.5k+ stars), mature, long-running project, primary reference implementation for Usenet client APIs
architecture: Monolithic Python app with an embedded web server. All operations go through a single endpoint (/sabnzbd/api) dispatched by a mode query parameter (mode=queue, mode=history, mode=addurl, mode=addfile, mode=pause, mode=resume, mode=delete, mode=change_cat, mode=change_opts, mode=priority, ...), plus output=json for JSON instead of the legacy XML. Every call (except version/auth) requires an apikey query parameter - a single static, regenerable secret, no session/cookie concept at all.
standout_features: Mode-dispatch single-endpoint RPC style (?mode=X&...) rather than REST resources - simple to implement and simple to reverse-engineer/mock, but harder to document via OpenAPI
Priority is a small signed integer scale (-2 Paused, -1 Low, 0 Normal, 1 High, 2 Force, -100 'use category default') letting category defaults cascade unless explicitly overridden per job

Post-processing is an explicit numeric enum on the job (0 None, 1 +Repair, 2 +Repair/Unpack, 3 +Repair/Unpack/Delete) decoupled from the download itself - a distinct pipeline stage after the raw transfer completes

History is a first-class, separate query surface from the live queue (mode=history vs mode=queue), with its own retry/delete/mark_as_completed actions - completed/failed jobs don't just disappear, they move to an addressable history list, which is exactly what *arr-style import polling depends on
Category is a simple string tag (default '*') that maps to output folder + default priority + default post-processing script server-side
ideas_for_kurio: Introduce an explicit, separately-addressable 'history' surface in Kurio.Server (distinct from the live active-queue endpoint/hub) so completed/failed/cancelled downloads remain queryable after removal from the active queue - needed for both a dashboard 'history' tab and any future *arr-style completed-download-import polling
Add a small signed priority scale (or reuse an enum) plus a 'category' string that carries default output-path/priority/post-processing settings, mirroring SABnzbd's cascade-unless-overridden model

Model post-processing (checksum verification, unzip/move, notification webhook) as an explicit numbered pipeline stage attached to a job/category rather than folding it into the download engine itself - this maps well onto Kurio.Core's existing checksum-verification feature and leaves room for future 'unpack archive' or 'run script' steps
Keep a simple static API-key-only auth mode available for headless/automation use even if Kurio.Server later adds richer auth
pitfalls_to_avoid: Avoid SABnzbd's single-endpoint mode-dispatch style for Kurio's primary API - prefer proper REST resources for discoverability/OpenAPI, but it's fine to keep it in mind as a lowest-common-denominator compatibility shim if third-party *arr-only tools ever expect it
Don't let 'history' become unbounded - SABnzbd users routinely hit issues with huge history files; plan for retention/pruning from day one

name: NZBGet JSON-RPC API
popularity: Moderate but long-standing (~1k+ stars for the community fork), stable/maintained, lightweight C++ alternative to SABnzbd
architecture: Single process exposing XML-RPC, JSON-RPC, and JSON-P-RPC over one HTTP endpoint (/jsonrpc), all three protocols implementing an identical method set. Auth is plain HTTP Basic auth with three distinct credential tiers baked into config (ControlUsername/Password for full access, RestrictedUsername/Password for a read-mostly/no-settings-access role, AddUsername/Password for an add-only role limited to append + version). JSON-RPC here only supports positional (not named) parameters and does not support batched multicalls, unlike its XML-RPC sibling.
standout_features: Three-tier role-based Basic-auth credentials baked into the server config itself (full/restricted/add-only) rather than a single shared API key - a genuinely useful least-privilege pattern for exposing a 'submit only' credential to a browser extension or a *arr app without granting it settings access
append is the canonical 'submit a job' RPC (analogous to addurl/addfile), decoupled from listgroups/listfiles for querying live queue state and history for completed/failed jobs

pausedownload/resumedownload/pausepost/resumepost/pausescan/resumescan separate pause/resume controls per pipeline stage (download vs post-processing vs directory-scan) rather than one blanket pause flag
rate for global speed-limit adjustment and testserver/testserverspeed/testdiskspeed/testnetworkspeed as built-in diagnostics callable over the same RPC surface

Extension script management exposed as RPC methods themselves (loadextensions/downloadextension/updateextension/deleteextension) - post-processing/notification scripts are managed remotely through the API, not just dropped in a folder
ideas_for_kurio: Add a role-scoped API key tier to Kurio.Server (e.g. full-control key vs an add-only key meant for browser-extension handoff) so a browser extension or public-facing capture endpoint can be granted a narrowly-scoped credential instead of a full-access key
Separate pause/resume semantics by pipeline stage if/when Kurio adds post-processing (pause the transfer vs pause a pending checksum/move step) rather than one global paused bool
Expose built-in network/disk diagnostics endpoints (analogous to testserverspeed/testdiskspeed) for the dashboard's 'test this download source/connection' UX

Consider offering both a REST/JSON surface and (lower priority) a minimal RPC-style compatibility shim only if a concrete consumer needs it - NZBGet's JSON-RPC positional-params quirk is a good cautionary example of API ergonomics to avoid in Kurio's own native API
pitfalls_to_avoid: Don't require strictly positional parameters in Kurio's own JSON API the way NZBGet's JSON-RPC does - it makes client code fragile and hard to read; keep named JSON fields
HTTP Basic auth with credentials embedded in URLs (as NZBGet's docs show, http://user:pass@host/jsonrpc) leaks into logs/history easily - prefer header-based Bearer tokens for Kurio

name: Sonarr/Radarr 'download client' integration contract (Servarr ecosystem)
repo: Sonarr/Sonarr and Radarr/Radarr (contract documented via Servarr/Wiki)
popularity: Extremely high adoption as the de-facto standard PVR/media-automation stack; Sonarr ~14k+ stars, Radarr similar; both actively maintained
language: C#/.NET (Sonarr, Radarr) - directly relevant precedent since Kurio is also .NET
architecture: Sonarr/Radarr poll a configured 'download client' on an interval via that client's native API (qBittorrent, SABnzbd, NZBGet, Deluge, Transmission, etc. each have a dedicated adapter inside Sonarr/Radarr implementing a shared internal download-client interface). The contract each adapter must satisfy is: (1) accept a new job (magnet/URL/NZB) tagged with a category, (2) report a queue of in-progress items with enough per-item status/progress to render in the Activity/Queue UI, (3) retain completed items with a resolvable local output path/directory until Radarr/Sonarr has imported them ('Completed Download Handling' requires the client not to purge history before import), (4) support remote path mapping when the download client's filesystem view differs from the *arr app's (e.g. Docker container vs host, or Linux client + Windows *arr).
standout_features: 'Remote Path Mapping' as an explicit, separate settings concept: a dumb string search/replace applied to whatever path the download client reports, needed whenever the download client and the *arr app don't share an identical filesystem view (classic Docker-volume-mismatch problem)

'Completed Download Handling' hinges entirely on the download client keeping completed-job history (with a stable output path) available until the *arr app has scanned and imported it - premature history pruning breaks the integration silently

Because there's no single canonical *arr download-client API, third-party servers (rdt-client, and by precedent Kurio) get broadest compatibility for free by emulating an existing supported client's wire protocol (most commonly qBittorrent's) rather than lobbying for a new native integration to be coded into Sonarr/Radarr
Category assignment at add-time is the main hook *arr apps use to keep their own downloads segregated from user-added ones in the same client
ideas_for_kurio: Prioritize the qBittorrent-compatibility shim (see qBittorrent entry) as the concrete, lowest-effort path to real Sonarr/Radarr interoperability, rather than trying to get a native 'Kurio' adapter merged upstream into Sonarr/Radarr's C# codebase

When designing Kurio's own job model, include a stable, never-mutated 'final output path' field per job plus a documented retention window before a completed job is purged from history/state - this is the exact prerequisite Completed Download Handling needs

Add a first-class 'remote path mapping' concept to Kurio.Server config (host-path <-> container-path substitution table) since Kurio itself will often run in Docker while a *arr app or the dashboard's host filesystem view differs
Support a category/label field on job submission from day one (already loosely implied by Kurio.Core's design) and surface it in both the REST API and SignalR events
pitfalls_to_avoid: Don't purge job history immediately on completion - keep it until an explicit acknowledgment/import or a configurable retention timeout, or any future *arr-style consumer will race and miss files
Don't assume the consumer and Kurio.Server share a filesystem view; always design paths to be mappable/relative to a category root, not absolute host paths baked into responses

name: MeTube
popularity: High for its niche (~7k+ stars), actively maintained, extremely popular in the self-hosted/yt-dlp community
architecture: Single-container app: a Python backend wrapping yt-dlp, an Angular SPA served by the same process, and WebSocket-based real-time status pushed to the UI (no polling) - directly analogous to Kurio.Server's SignalR hub pushing progress to Kurio.Web. State is plain JSON files on disk in a configurable STATE_DIR (queue.json, pending.json, completed.json, subscriptions.json) rather than a database, giving trivial backup/inspection/portability. Downloads land in DOWNLOAD_DIR (optionally split further via AUDIO_DOWNLOAD_DIR and CUSTOM_DIRS subfolders), with a TEMP_DIR for in-progress files recommended to be a tmpfs/RAM mount for performance.
standout_features: PUID/PGID/UMASK environment variables plus a CHOWN_DIRS toggle so the container can run as an arbitrary host UID/GID and correctly own files on bind-mounted volumes - the standard self-hosted-NAS permission story
Deliberate separation of queue.json (pending/active) vs completed.json (finished/failed) state files, letting the UI and any external tooling distinguish 'still working' vs 'done' without a database
CLEAR_COMPLETED_AFTER auto-purge delay for the completed list, balancing history visibility against unbounded growth

URL_PREFIX support specifically for reverse-proxy base-path deployment (e.g. https://host/metube/), and CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS specifically to let browser extensions/bookmarklets call the API cross-origin from arbitrary tab origins
MAX_CONCURRENT_DOWNLOADS as a simple, single global concurrency knob exposed as an env var, not buried in a config file
ideas_for_kurio: Adopt PUID/PGID/UMASK env vars (with an optional auto-chown-on-start step) in Kurio's Dockerfile/entrypoint so the container can write into NAS bind mounts (Synology/Unraid/TrueNAS) with correct host ownership - currently a gap since Kurio only has a web dashboard and no documented container image

Add a documented URL_PREFIX / PathBase-style base-path config to Kurio.Server (ASP.NET Core has native UsePathBase support) so Kurio can be reverse-proxied at a subpath without breaking SignalR negotiation

Add a narrowly-scoped CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS setting (default empty/deny) explicitly documented as 'set this to enable a browser-extension or bookmarklet capture flow' - this is the direct alternative to native messaging for a web-facing download server

Mirror the queue.json/completed.json file-split pattern for Kurio.Core's own JSON state persistence if not already split - keeps the 'hot' active-queue state file small and fast to read/write independent of a potentially large history file
Expose a CLEAR_COMPLETED_AFTER-equivalent retention policy for Kurio's job history
pitfalls_to_avoid: Don't couple TEMP_DIR/incomplete-file location to the same volume as the final DOWNLOAD_DIR by default - document that using a separate fast/tmpfs mount for in-progress segments avoids slow bind-mount NAS writes during active transfers

Don't require a database for state just because Kurio.Core already does JSON persistence - keep parity with the lightweight file-based model for easy backup/restore, consistent with what Kurio.Core already does

name: linuxserver.io Docker image conventions
repo: linuxserver/docker-baseimage-alpine / linuxserver/docker-documentation (ecosystem convention, not a single app)
popularity: Extremely high adoption across the self-hosted ecosystem (thousands of images built on this convention); the de-facto packaging standard people expect on Unraid/Synology/TrueNAS app catalogs
language: Shell/s6-overlay init system, applies to images of any backend language
architecture: Each image runs an internal fixed user 'abc' (uid/gid 911 baked in at build time); at container start, the s6-overlay init system reads PUID/PGID env vars and rewrites abc's uid/gid to match, then chowns the app's own files (not necessarily user volumes) before exec'ing the real process as that user. Every image exposes a single, consistently-named /config volume for all app state/settings/logs/db, keeping every other data volume (media, downloads, etc.) separate and app-specific. Health is normally surfaced via a docker HEALTHCHECK hitting the app's own HTTP endpoint.
standout_features: Fixed internal uid/gid (911) is a documented ecosystem-wide constant across all linuxserver.io images, making cross-image volume permission reasoning predictable

Strict separation of concerns between the one true /config volume (settings/db/logs) versus arbitrary user-mounted data volumes (e.g. /downloads, /media) - this single convention is what lets Unraid/Synology/TrueNAS app templates auto-generate sensible default mount points
s6-overlay as process supervisor inside the container (handles PUID/PGID remap, signal forwarding, graceful shutdown, and optional multiple co-processes) rather than a bare ENTRYPOINT script
HEALTHCHECK baked into the image itself (not left to the user's compose file) so orchestrators (Portainer, Unraid, Synology Container Manager) show accurate health status out of the box
ideas_for_kurio: Publish a Kurio.Server Docker image following this exact convention: internal service user with PUID/PGID remap support, a single /config volume for Kurio's JSON state/settings, and separate documented volumes for /downloads/incomplete and /downloads/complete

Add a Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK hitting a lightweight Kurio.Server /health or /api/health endpoint (ASP.NET Core has built-in health check middleware) so container orchestrators report accurate status without extra user config

Write Unraid Community Applications / Synology / TrueNAS SCALE app-catalog templates once the Docker image is stable - these all key off documented volume paths and env vars, which is exactly what MeTube/linuxserver.io establish as expected norms

Document a stable, minimal set of env vars (PUID, PGID, UMASK, PORT, API_KEY, DOWNLOAD_DIR, INCOMPLETE_DIR) as Kurio's public Docker contract, mirroring what users already expect from every other self-hosted download tool
pitfalls_to_avoid: Don't chown large media/download volumes recursively on every container start (slow on NAS with huge libraries) - only chown the app's own /config and let PUID/PGID be applied to the process user for new files going forward, as linuxserver.io images are careful to scope their chown operations narrowly

Don't run as root by default even though it's the path of least resistance - the entire PUID/PGID convention exists because self-hosters mount NAS shares with specific host-side uid/gid and expect the container to respect that, not require running privileged

name: Browser native messaging handoff (WebExtensions spec + MyJDownloader/FDM/Gopeed patterns)
repo: WebExtensions Native Messaging spec (Chrome/Firefox/Edge docs) plus GopeedLab/browser-extension, magnetgrouplabs/myjdownloader-extension-mv3
popularity: Native messaging itself is a stable, long-standing cross-browser standard; the download-manager extensions built on it (FDM, Gopeed, JDownloader Interceptor) are each moderately popular niche tools
language: JSON manifest + JS extension + a native stdio-speaking host binary in any language
architecture: Three distinct architectures observed: (1) MyJDownloader's official extension does NOT use native messaging at all - it relays entirely through MyJDownloader's cloud relay service to a JDownloader instance that maintains an outbound connection to that cloud, avoiding CORS/localhost issues entirely at the cost of requiring a cloud account and internet round-trip; (2) the separate 'JDownloader Interceptor' extension and FDM's extension use classic WebExtensions native messaging - the browser launches a native host process declared by an OS-level manifest file (registry key on Windows, well-known directory on macOS/Linux) with type: stdio, allowed_origins/allowed_extensions restricting which extension IDs may connect, and exchange length-prefixed JSON messages (4-byte native-endian length header + UTF-8 JSON body, host->browser capped at 1MB, browser->host capped at 1MB-4GB depending on browser/version) over the child process's stdin/stdout; the extension intercepts chrome.downloads.onCreated / context-menu clicks, cancels the browser's own download, captures cookies/referrer/headers via the extension APIs, and forwards a job description JSON to the native host, which then talks to the actual download manager (often over a local loopback HTTP/RPC port, not further native-messaging hops); (3) Gopeed's extension instead talks directly over HTTP to Gopeed's own always-listening local REST server (default http://localhost:9999), or to a configured remote Gopeed server, entirely sidestepping native messaging - CORS is handled by Gopeed's server explicitly allowing the extension's origin.
standout_features: Native messaging manifest keyed by exact extension ID (allowed_extensions for Chrome, allowed_origins style for Firefox) - a strict allowlist so no arbitrary web page or extension can spawn/talk to the native host

Length-prefixed newline-free JSON framing over stdio is intentionally simple and easy to implement in any language (a 4-byte little/native-endian length header, then that many bytes of UTF-8 JSON) - no HTTP server, no port, no firewall exposure at all

FDM/Bolt-style flow of intercepting chrome.downloads.onCreated, cancelling the native browser download, and re-submitting with captured cookies+referrer+headers is the standard technique for handing a fully-authenticated download context to an external manager

Gopeed's simpler alternative: skip native messaging entirely and just run a persistent local HTTP server with a scoped CORS allowlist - trades OS-level install complexity (manifest registration) for a more familiar REST/CORS security model

MyJDownloader's cloud-relay pattern demonstrates a third option entirely: no localhost/CORS/native-host complexity at all, but requires the download server to maintain a persistent outbound connection to a broker service and requires user account/pairing setup
ideas_for_kurio: For a first browser-extension milestone, prefer Gopeed's approach over native messaging: have Kurio.Server expose a small, explicitly-CORS-allowlisted 'capture' REST endpoint (e.g. POST /api/capture with url/referrer/cookies/headers) on its existing local/LAN port, since Kurio.Server already runs as a persistent server (unlike JDownloader which is often a desktop app) - this avoids the OS-level native-messaging-manifest installation step entirely and fits Kurio's server-first architecture

Design the extension to intercept chrome.downloads.onCreated (and a context-menu 'Download with Kurio' action), cancel the browser's native download, capture cookies/referrer/custom headers via the WebRequest/cookies APIs, and POST that job description to Kurio.Server's capture endpoint - directly modeled on the FDM/Bolt flow

If a future desktop-agent story returns, offer native messaging as the alternative transport for users running Kurio purely as a local desktop process without a reachable HTTP port - reuse the same JSON job-description schema over the length-prefixed stdio framing instead of HTTP, so the extension-side code barely changes

Require a per-install pairing token (generated in the Kurio.Web dashboard, entered once into the extension's options page) rather than open CORS-to-any-origin, to avoid a hostile webpage silently POSTing arbitrary download jobs to a LAN-reachable Kurio.Server

Explicitly design the capture payload schema (url, filename hint, referrer, cookies[], extra headers{}, suggested category) now, even before an extension exists, since it will also double as the schema for a future 'add via clipboard/bookmarklet' capture path
pitfalls_to_avoid: Don't default to Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * on any authenticated Kurio.Server endpoint just to make a browser extension work - scope CORS to the specific extension origin (chrome-extension://<id>) or require a pairing token in addition to CORS

Don't build native messaging first as the primary transport - it requires a per-OS installer step (registry keys on Windows, manifest files in specific directories on macOS/Linux) that adds real deployment friction for a server-first product like Kurio; keep it as an optional secondary transport only if a local-desktop-agent use case materializes
Remember native messaging's hard message-size ceiling (1MB) if that path is ever built - don't try to pass large payloads (e.g. embedded file blobs) through it, only pass small job-description JSON
